research.topic: Mumbai, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (CSMIA), Terminal 2 (opened 2014): architecture, structure, art programme and visual signatures

claims.claim: Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) designed T2, with Roger Duffy as design partner. SOM was also the structural and MEP engineer (Charles Besjak, structural director; Preetam Biswas, structural engineer). Larsen & Toubro was architect and engineer of record and the EPC contractor. GVK / Mumbai International Airport Ltd (MIAL) was the client.
claims.detail: Fashion designers Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla are credited for 'Cultural Design Collaboration' on aspects of the interiors. Other credits: Brandston Partnership (lighting), Pentagram and Entro (signage), BNP Associates (baggage), Cerami & Associates (acoustics), Formglas (GFRG coffers and column cladding), Lindner (metal ceilings), CH2M HILL (programme management), Robert Polidori (photography). L&T's EPC award is dated November 2007. No landscape architect is credited on SOM's or ArchDaily's pages; Airport Technology lists HED for interior landscape.
claims.design_takeaway: The Mumbai 'DNA' is the work of a global firm combined with an Indian cultural collaborator. ZMI can credit its Mumbai layer the same way: an engineered long-span system dressed in Indian craft references.

claims.claim: Prime Minister Manmohan Singh inaugurated T2 on 10 January 2014. International operations moved into T2 on 12 February 2014, and the old international terminal closed the same day. SOM lists 2010 as design finish and 2014 as completion.
claims.detail: Construction began around 2008 (Airport Technology), and the terminal had to be built in phases on the site of the existing terminal, which stayed operational. One 2014 news piece says T2 had originally been scheduled to open in 2010 (seen in a search snippet only, The Peninsula; not opened).
claims.design_takeaway: The 2014 opening gives ZMI's narrative a firm date: the Mumbai DNA is a decade-old 'new' terminal. A returning passenger's memory of it dates from 2014 onward.

claims.claim: T2 is a four-storey integrated domestic and international terminal designed for 40 million passengers a year. Its gross floor area is about 4.4 million sq ft (about 410,000 m2).
claims.detail: Floor-area figures disagree. SOM press releases and PTI give 4.4 million sq ft, 4.39 lakh m2 or about 410,000 m2; the TRB/ACRP abstract also gives 410,000 m2. SOM's current project page gives 450,000 m2 and Architect Magazine gives about 4.8 million sq ft. SOM's AIA announcement wrongly says '450,000-square-foot'. Building height is 36 m on SOM's project page and 45 m per Airport Technology. Operating figures from PTI/Business Today (Jan 2014): 9,900 peak-hour passengers, 188 check-in counters, 52 boarding gates, 47 escalators, 73 elevators, 10 baggage carousels. SPS Airbuz gives 208 check-in counters. SOM says the design 'had to triple the airport's capacity' and has 29 gates (likely contact-gate positions, not the 52 bridges).
claims.design_takeaway: 40 Mppa is Mumbai's contribution to ZMI's combined-capacity target. Use about 410,000 m2 and 4 levels as the BOM reference module when sizing ZMI's merged headhouse.

claims.claim: T2's reported cost varies between sources. The best-supported figure for the terminal is about Rs 5,200 to 5,500 crore (about US$894m), with a reported 32% cost escalation.
claims.detail: Reported figures: Rs 5,200 crore (SPS Airbuz); Rs 5,500 crore with 32% escalation (Outlook Business); US$894.3m (Airport Technology, mislabelled there as 'INR5.5bn', but US$894m is about Rs 5,500 crore at roughly 61.5 INR/USD in Jan 2014, my arithmetic); Rs 9,800 crore with 32% escalation (PTI via Business Today); Rs 12,500 crore 'estimated project cost' (Business Today photo feature, which appears to cover the whole airport rebuild). None of these is an audited figure.
claims.design_takeaway: Do not quote a single cost in the design document. Give the Rs 5,200 to 5,500 crore range and footnote the higher figures as wider-programme numbers.

claims.claim: The headhouse is covered by a single long-span steel-truss roof of about 70,000 m2 (753,475 sq ft). SOM describes it as 'one of the world's largest roofs without an expansion joint'.
claims.detail: The 'largest without an expansion joint' claim originates with SOM and is repeated by the TRB/ACRP abstract, STRUCTURE magazine, e-architect and World Architecture. It is a self-described superlative, not an independently ranked one. According to a World Architecture summary, the roof is separated from the base structures so it can move with temperature. Other dimensions: Architect Magazine (search snippet only) gives a '1,150-foot-by-900-foot roof' (about 350 x 274 m, roughly 96,000 m2 as a bounding rectangle, so larger than 70,000 m2; it probably includes canopy overhangs or describes the envelope). Formglas (search snippet) says the coffered ceiling below is 50,000 m2 (540,000 sq ft). Business Today says the steel in 'the two roofs' would build two Eiffel Towers. SPS Airbuz and Infrastructure Today give '11-acre' (about 44,500 m2) for the mega roof, which conflicts with 70,000 m2.
claims.design_takeaway: An unbroken roof plane is a legitimate Mumbai signature. ZMI's Mumbai-derived zone (for example the check-in hall) could read as one continuous coffered roof field with no visible joints.

claims.claim: The roof stands on only 30 composite (concrete-encased steel) mega-columns on a 64 m (N-S) x 34 m (E-W) grid, about 210 ft x 112 ft. The trusses are only about 4 m (13 ft) deep, deepen near the columns, and run in both orthogonal and 45-degree grids. The roof cantilevers 40 m (131 ft) at the perimeter.
claims.detail: STRUCTURE magazine (snippet) compares the orthogonal truss system to a two-way flat slab. Column height: SOM press releases say 'thirty 130-foot columns' or 'thirty 40-meter columns'; Formglas/e-architect say 'over 100 feet high'. Architect Magazine (snippet) gives clear spans of '111- and 210-foot'. All sources agree on 30 columns.
claims.design_takeaway: A 64 x 34 m column grid with 40 m cantilevers is a concrete, game-buildable parameter. ZMI's Mumbai-derived hall can use a wide rectangular grid of a few huge columns, in contrast with a denser grid from the other two airports.

claims.claim: The mega-columns were designed to work as hoists, so the whole roof was built without tower cranes while the existing terminal stayed in operation next door.
claims.detail: STRUCTURE magazine (search snippet) says individual 'column pods' were built on top of a peripheral mega-column and then moved to their final positions on temporary erection trusses. ArchDaily captions mention a 'column pod top node connection' model.
claims.design_takeaway: This is a narrative detail ZMI can use in its construction-phase backstory or game lore: roof modules ('pods') raised up their own columns.

claims.claim: The design concept is the peacock, India's national bird. The client GVK set it as the brief, and SOM took the iridescent, teardrop-shaped 'eye' of the tail feather as the motif for the coffered ceiling and column cladding.
claims.detail: SOM's own release ties the peacock to the coloured glass: 'The constellation of colours makes reference to the peacock, the national bird of India, and the symbol of the airport.' GVK's design head (Chintan Shukla, interviewed by MGS Architecture) says the brief was 'the most beautiful mascot of our country - the peacock'. Indian press (PTI, Business Today) described the terminal as 'inspired by a dancing peacock'. GVK-sourced press (SPS Airbuz, Infrastructure Today, March 2014) says the check-in hall is 'inspired by 1,000 white peacocks in the sky'. That phrase is promotional and I found no SOM source for it. Apollo (Feb 2014) reported a planned white automated peacock puppet that would 'fly' a circle on the hour; I did not verify whether it was installed.
claims.design_takeaway: The peacock-feather eye is the strongest single Mumbai motif. In ZMI, render it abstractly as teardrop or oval coffers with a coloured lens at the centre, not as literal birds.

claims.claim: The ceiling is a field of more than 4,000 moulded coffers, each about 100 sq ft (about 9.3 m2). Each coffer has a round aperture holding a coloured dichroic or laminated glass lens. Daylight from skylights above, and electric light at night, passes through the lenses and speckles the hall floor with coloured spots.
claims.detail: SOM: 'Small disks of colourful glass recessed within the canopy's coffers speckle the hall below with light.' World Architecture: a laminated lens gives 'two colours, depending on the angle at which light strikes it'. GVK's design head calls it 'circular DICHROIC glass in each GFRC and GFRG module', with a large roof-level skylight that 'filters the sunlight in a spectrum of various colors similar to that of a peacock feather'. One search summary gives a standard coffer of 2.8 x 2.7 m (about 7.6 m2), which is smaller than 100 sq ft; I could not trace that figure to an opened page. Infrastructure Today lists '30,000 sq ft skylight glass'.
claims.design_takeaway: The coloured-light 'confetti' on the floor is the most recognisable sensory memory of T2. ZMI can reproduce it as a daylight-driven shader or particle effect in the Mumbai-derived zone that shifts colour with sun angle and time of day.

claims.claim: The columns are tapered, 'mushrooming' forms. Their coffered cladding runs continuously up the shaft and flares into the ceiling plane, so column and roof read as one surface. The design was meant to flow 'from the vertical' to 'the horizontal ceiling pattern', like a feather.
claims.detail: Skylights sit at the column capitals, which 'swoop up' into the ceiling (Formglas via World Architects, search snippet only). The capitals were the most complex part of the job, about one third of roughly 15,000 GFRG parts, made from nearly 500 CNC-milled moulds (another source: more than 500 moulds and 15,500 components). Column cladding modules weigh about 500 to 1,000 kg each and are fixed to a steel cage around the RCC column core (GVK design head). Architect Magazine (snippet) reportedly gives capitals about 111 ft wide, which I could not verify. Formglas's own page lists dichroic light lenses lit from above by day and artificially at night (search snippet). The form is a flaring capital (mushroom/tree), not literal branching.
claims.design_takeaway: For ZMI, the Mumbai column is a single trunk that flares into a coffered canopy with a skylight ring at its crown. Model it as a continuous surface, not a column plus capital plus ceiling, and put a light source at the top of each column.

claims.claim: SOM and the press describe the column-and-coffer grid as recalling the carved stone mandapas (pillared pavilions) of Hindu temples and traditional Indian pavilions. Jali screens add an Indo-Islamic reference.
claims.detail: Architect Magazine (search snippet only): 'the grid of columns and ceiling coffers recalls the intricately carved stone mandapas, or pavilions, of ancient Hindu temples.' Dezeen and SOM text say the canopy references traditional pavilions. SOM's project text cites 'the articulated coffered treatment on the headhouse columns and roof surfaces' and 'intricate jali window screens that filter dappled light into the concourses' as integrated regional patterns.
claims.design_takeaway: Mumbai's 'mandapa under a peacock canopy' reading suits ZMI as the ceremonial pillared hall where the three DNA strands meet.

claims.claim: T2 has a compact, elongated X-shaped plan. Retail, dining and a large baggage system sit at the centre of the X, and four concourses (piers) radiate out to maximise aircraft frontage. Gates can swing between domestic and international use as demand shifts.
claims.detail: SOM and the AIA citation say the X fits a tight site, avoiding surrounding informal settlements, the overflowing Mithi River and immovable historic monuments, and it had to rise in phases over the operating old terminal. SOM text adds that the 'radiating piers permit the shortest possible walking distances'. A 2024 airport guide (low-quality, not opened) mentions 4 piers and 52 aerobridges.
claims.design_takeaway: Mumbai's contribution to ZMI's geometry could be the stacked central core with radiating piers. If ZMI already has a different pier form, mark Mumbai's X with four arms in the merged plan.

claims.claim: T2 is a four-level vertically stacked terminal. A grand processing 'headhouse' (check-in hall) sits on top of modular concourses. All international and domestic departing passengers enter the headhouse at Level 4.
claims.detail: Level allocation per Airport Technology and Infrastructure Today (March 2014): Level 1, ground transportation; Level 2, arrivals (10 carousels, 72 immigration counters); Level 3, domestic security and retail hub; Level 4, check-in, international security and retail (the headhouse). SOM text: 'interconnecting light slots and multi-story light wells' bring daylight down to lower floors. Dezeen gives check-in space as about 50,000 m2 (also Business Today: 'about 50,000 sq meters of check-in space').
claims.design_takeaway: ZMI can make 'arrive at the top, under the peacock roof' the Mumbai ceremony: departures drop-off at the highest level straight into the big hall, with arrivals below.

claims.claim: A dedicated elevated road, the Sahar Elevated Access Road, carries traffic signal-free from the Western Express Highway to T2's upper-level forecourt. It opened in February 2014 together with T2's international operations. The 40 m roof cantilever extends over the arrivals roadway to shelter passengers from heat and monsoon rain.
claims.detail: Length disagrees: Gulf News gives '2.2km elevated Sahar corridor'; SPS Airbuz and Infrastructure Today give a 'dedicated six-lane 3.2-km elevated expressway'. Wikipedia (pointer only) gives about 2.2 km with three lanes each way. Gulf News reports cost as Rs 4 billion and a saving of about 30 minutes; a search result gives Rs 400.77 crore shared by the central and state governments, MMRDA and MIAL. SOM: curbside drop-off sized for large groups of well-wishers. Multi-level car park for 5,200 cars.
claims.design_takeaway: The elevated approach ramp plus a deep cantilevered canopy over the kerb is a Mumbai arrival gesture ZMI can reuse at its departures kerb, with a canopy coffered on its underside so the peacock pattern starts outdoors.

claims.claim: The check-in hall is wrapped in a 50-ft (about 15 m) tall glass cable-stayed wall, which SOM calls 'the longest in the world'. The exterior soffits and cladding are glass-fibre-reinforced concrete (GFRC), carrying the coffer pattern outside the glass line.
claims.detail: Dezeen gives 'A 900-metre long glass wall with a gridded cable frame'; SOM and the TRB abstract say 'the largest and longest cable wall system in the world' without a length. Both are self-reported superlatives. Perforated metal panels on the curtain wall filter low east and west sun, and the glazing has a custom frit pattern. GFRC was made in Hong Kong/China; interior GFRG was made by Formglas in Canada and Mexico. The groove lines of the outer GFRC and inner GFRG ceilings had to line up across the glass wall (GVK design head).
claims.design_takeaway: In ZMI, run the coffered ceiling straight through a tall frameless glass wall so the canopy reads the same inside and out. This is a cheap but strong visual cue in both 2D and 3D renders.

claims.claim: T2's passive and daylight strategy combines: skylights across the check-in hall (claimed to cut terminal energy use by 23%), light slots and multi-storey light wells for lower floors, jali screens on concourse windows, perforated metal sun-screening and fritted glazing on east and west faces, daylight-responsive lighting controls, and the 40 m shading cantilever over the kerb.
claims.detail: The 23% figure is SOM's projection at opening ('will reduce'), not a measured result. BD+C notes inconsistent wording (check-in hall versus entrance hall). No measured post-occupancy figure was found.
claims.design_takeaway: For ZMI near Nagpur (hot, high-sun site), the Mumbai layer supplies a toplight-plus-screen strategy: small coloured apertures in a deep coffered roof, jali on the facades, deep canopies. It reads as both heritage and climate response.

claims.claim: T2 received LEED Gold (BD+C New Construction) on opening. Later, the Indian Green Building Council certified it as a 'Platinum rated Green Existing Building' for 2016–2019 and again for 2021–2024.
claims.detail: A LEED news item (search snippet only, Travel Trends Today) cites a 42.58% water-use reduction through grey-water reuse and efficient fixtures. Measures reported with the IGBC recertification (Asian Aviation, 10 Jan 2022): onsite solar of 5,310,141 kWh (about 6.6% of net consumption), LED retrofit, EC fans in AHUs, IoT temperature sensors, a sewage treatment plant reusing water for cooling towers and horticulture, and 229 rainwater-harvesting pits.
claims.design_takeaway: Useful benchmark for ZMI's sustainability claims. The operational IGBC rating is a more credible comparison than the LEED design rating.

claims.claim: The verifiable interior palette is white or off-white moulded ceilings and columns (GFRG), dotted with multicoloured glass lenses. Other elements include custom lotus-inspired chandeliers, traditional mirror-mosaic work by local artists, jali screens, wood-look powder-coated metal ceilings (Lindner, about 120,000 m2) and extensive granite flooring.
claims.detail: I could not verify a 'white and gold' scheme for the terminal as a whole. The gold references found apply to the GVK Lounge ('Level 4 decked out in a gold theme, while the silver theme flows through Level 3', TheDesignAir, search snippet only). Infrastructure Today (GVK-sourced) gives '1,000 lotus-inspired chandeliers' and '1.85 million sq ft of granite'. The 'white' reading is supported by '1,000 white peacocks' marketing and photo descriptions. The lounge material was not opened, so treat 'gold' as lounge-specific.
claims.design_takeaway: For the Mumbai layer, use white sculpted surfaces plus jewel-coloured point lights (peacock blue, green, gold) and lotus chandeliers. Reserve gold as an accent, not the base colour, unless further evidence appears.

claims.claim: The art programme 'Jaya He' (GVK New Museum) was curated and designed by scenographer Rajeev Sethi for GVK's Sanjay Reddy. It is commonly described as a multi-storey Art Wall about 3 km long, lit by skylights, and the airport calls it 'arguably India's largest public art initiative'.
claims.detail: Length: 3 km (PTI/Business Today, Apollo, Khaleej Times, Scroll.in) or 'over 3.2km of wall space spanning the terminal's four levels' (Moodie Davitt Report). Height: '18-metre high walls' (Khaleej Times) or 60 ft from skylight to floor (Moodie Davitt). The largest installation covers about 80,000 sq ft (Apollo). Number of works varies widely: 'over 7,000 artefacts collected from over 1,500 artists' (PTI, Khaleej Times); 'more than 2,000 pieces of art, artifacts and crafts' (Moodie Davitt); 'approximately 3000 ethnographic objects' (Heritage Lab, 2016). The 7,000 figure appears to be an opening-day promotional number. Heritage Lab says Reddy envisioned the project in 2009. Apollo says more than 100 restorers prepared works.
claims.design_takeaway: A km-scale curated wall along the passenger route is Mumbai's cultural signature. ZMI can inherit it as a museum spine, possibly re-hosting 'transferred' works from all three closed airports, which is a strong merger story beat.

claims.claim: Jaya He is organised along the passenger route in three parts: 'Thresholds of India' on the central curving wall through departures, 'Layered Narratives' (Mumbai-themed commissions) along the arrivals corridor's moving walkways towards baggage claim, and 'Baggage Acclaimed' on the carousels.
claims.detail: Thresholds of India: about 70 installations (Moodie Davitt) in six themes: India Greets, India Seamless, India Moves, India Elemental, India Global, India's Silent Sentinels (Moodie Davitt, Heritage Lab, Scroll.in). The official CSIA page describes the central wall as 'a central curvilinear spine, designed to direct and control circulation of passengers through the terminal'. Layered Narratives: 32 commissioned works (Heritage Lab) or 'more than 20 contemporary Indian artists' (Moodie Davitt), mapping Mumbai as an unfolding urban narrative (Bollywood, finance and city life per Khaleej Times). Artists include Gigi Scaria, Manjunath Kamath, Jagannath Panda, Gulammohammed Sheikh and Alexis Kersey. Baggage Acclaimed: four sculptural textile and costume installations on the carousels (Heritage Lab). The official page says only 'two distinct sections so far', so the third part may have been added later.
claims.design_takeaway: Use the art wall as wayfinding: a curved spine that guides departing passengers, a city-story gallery on the arrivals walkway, and a 'welcome' moment at reclaim. In ZMI's game this maps onto passenger-flow zones and could affect a satisfaction metric.

claims.detail: This list is my synthesis of which features recur across SOM, Dezeen, BD+C, World Architecture, Business Today, Moodie Davitt and Apollo. No survey of passenger recognition was found. Robert Polidori's widely published photographs centre on the coffered columns and ceiling.

Any two of these at full scale should make a returning Mumbai flyer think 'T2'.

open_questions: Exact roof plan dimensions: SOM and TRB give 70,000 m2, Architect Magazine (snippet) gives 1,150 x 900 ft, Formglas gives a 50,000 m2 ceiling, and GVK-sourced press gives '11 acres'. Which footprint does each figure measure? Open the Architect Magazine and STRUCTURE articles (403/404 when fetched) or the TRB paper PDF.
Are the coffer lenses true dichroic glass (GVK design head, Formglas) or laminated coloured glass (World Architecture)? Which colours are used, and is there one oculus per coffer or only in some?
Exact form of the column-top skylights (an oculus ring at each capital versus clustered openings) and the reported capital width of about 111 ft. This needs photos or SOM drawings.
Overall interior palette: 'white and gold' is unverified. Gold is documented only for the GVK lounge. Needs photo-based or first-hand confirmation.

Jaya He's current state after the 2021 change of airport operator (GVK to Adani, not verified here): have works been removed, reduced or rearranged? Is 'Baggage Acclaimed' still installed? Which count (7,000 / 3,000 / 2,000) reflects what is actually on display?
Length and lane count of the Sahar Elevated Access Road: 2.2 km (Gulf News) versus 3.2 km six-lane (SPS Airbuz, Infrastructure Today).
Authoritative T2-only cost: Rs 5,200 crore, Rs 5,500 crore, Rs 9,800 crore or Rs 12,500 crore. A MIAL annual report or AERA tariff order would settle it.
The renaming from CSIA to CSMIA (Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj) and the date domestic operations moved into T2 were not verified in this pass.

verdicts.corrected_claim: T2's reported cost varies widely, from Rs 5,200 crore to Rs 12,500 crore. The most often repeated terminal figure is about Rs 5,500 crore (about US$894m; £540m), with a reported 32% cost escalation. PTI, however, explicitly attributes Rs 9,800 crore to T2 itself, so the higher figure cannot simply be dismissed as a whole-airport number.
verdicts.note: All four cited figures are confirmed: Outlook Business ₹5,500 crore and 32% escalation; SPS Airbuz Rs 5,200 crore; PTI/Business Today 'T2 has come up at a whopping investment of Rs 9,800 crore' with 'over 32 per cent cost escalation'; Business Today photo feature 'estimated project cost of Rs 12,500 crore'. SOM's own 'In the Press' item (11 Feb 2014) also gives 'Rs5,500 crore (£540m)'. The Peninsula/AFP calls the wider revamp '$2bn'. Calling Rs 5,200 to 5,500 crore 'best-supported' is a judgement. PTI applies the same 32% escalation to Rs 9,800 crore and labels it T2, so the scope of each figure is unresolved.

It opened in February 2014 together with T2's international operations; its length is reported as 2.2 km (Gulf News) or 3.2 km six-lane (GVK-sourced press). The headhouse roof, which cantilevers up to 40 m at its perimeter, extends over the entire 'arrivals roadway' to shelter passengers from heat and monsoon rain.
verdicts.note: Gulf News confirms the 2.2 km length, Rs 4 billion cost (consistent with the Rs 400.77 crore search figure) and about 30 minutes saved. SPS Airbuz and Infrastructure Today confirm the 3.2 km six-lane figure. A search summary (Wikipedia-derived, unverified) says the road was built in two parts, about 1.8 km by MMRDA and about 1.5 km by MIAL, which may explain the discrepancy. SOM, Dezeen and World Architecture say the roof covers the 'entire arrivals roadway'. Tying the specific 40 m figure to the kerb is a reasonable inference, not a direct statement. Note that SOM's 'arrivals roadway' is the vehicle drop-off at the terminal, not the Level 2 arrivals hall. The 5,200-car, nine-storey car park is confirmed by Business Today. 'Signal-free' and 'large groups of well-wishers' were not verified.

claims.claim: T2 was designed by the New York office of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) for Bangalore International Airport Limited (BIAL). Grant Associates (UK) did the landscape architecture and fashion designers Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla (AJSK) did the interiors, furnishings and planter design. Larsen & Toubro was general contractor and Arup did MEP/fire engineering for T2. SOM did the structural engineering itself.
claims.detail: SOM design partners: Roger Duffy and Colin Koop. Managing partner: Laura Ettelman. Design principals: Peter Lefkovits and Derek A.R. Moore. Structural engineers (SOM): Preetam Biswas, Charles Besjak and others. Buro Happold did MEP for the multimodal transit hub; STUP did landside infrastructure; BNP Associates did baggage. L&T's construction contract was Rs 30.36bn (about US$413m), awarded October 2018.
claims.design_takeaway: Two of ZMI's three source buildings (CSMIA T2 and KIA T2) come from the same SOM New York practice (see blr-15). ZMI can present them as two chapters by one design family: Mumbai sculptural, Bengaluru orthogonal and botanical.

claims.claim: SOM's design was unveiled on 2 April 2019 with a first-phase target of March 2021. Construction began in 2019. PM Narendra Modi inaugurated T2 on 11 November 2022. Domestic operations began on 15 January 2023, with Star Air as the only airline that day. International operations began on 12 September 2023, after a postponement from 31 August 2023.
claims.detail: The first international arrival was Saudia SV866 from Jeddah at 10:15 on 12 Sep 2023. The first Indian carrier's international departure was IndiGo 6E1167 to Colombo. After the switch, T2 took all international flights plus domestic flights of AirAsia, Air India, Star Air and Vistara. AirAsia India moved its domestic flights to T2 in February 2023. Architectural Record gives the 'completion date' as September 2023. SOM's project page says 'construction complete, 2023'.
claims.design_takeaway: ZMI's backstory can mirror this phasing: the hall opens first, domestic traffic moves in next, and international traffic follows months later. That staging could also become game content, with opening phases as levels.

claims.claim: Phase 1 of T2 is about 255,000 m² over four levels. A separate 123,000 m² multimodal transit hub (MMTH) adjoins it. Together they come to roughly 380,000 m² (4.1 million sq ft).
claims.detail: Exact figures vary by source. SOM's 2024 release gives 255,000 m². BIAL, via Moodie Davitt and Airport Technology, gives 255,661 m². Grant Associates gives 255,645 m². Architectural Record gives 2.75 million sq ft (about 255,500 m²). SOM's project fact sheet lists 'building gross area 380,000 m²', which matches T2 plus the MMTH (255k + 123k). Architectural Record gives 4.1 million sq ft including the hub (about 381,000 m²).
claims.design_takeaway: Use 255,000 m² as the 'Bengaluru module' when sizing ZMI's processor zones. Treat the MMTH as a separate landside building linked to the terminal, a parti ZMI can reuse for its rail and metro interchange.

claims.claim: T2 Phase 1 handles 25 million passengers per year (mppa), of which SOM says about 20 mppa is international. Sources disagree on how much Phase 2 adds. For scale, the whole airport (T1 + T2) handled 41.88 million passengers in FY2024-25.
claims.detail: SOM's Derek Moore says the second phase would add another 10 mppa. BIAL CEO Hari Marar (The Week, May 2023) says Phase 2 will take T2 to 45 mppa and BIAL's total capacity to nearly 80 mppa. SOM's project page says capacity was 'doubled from 25 to 50 million' with room for another 20 million, but that figure appears to describe the airport as a whole. Traffic: 37.53m in FY24 and 41.88m in FY25 (36.05m domestic, 5.83m international). BIAL has reserved space for a T3 'by the late 2020s or early 2030s', targeting 90-100 mppa. I found no 2026 status update confirming whether Phase 2 is complete.
claims.design_takeaway: For ZMI's capacity model, KIA contributes about 42 mppa of real 2025 demand, against T2's design capacity of 25 mppa (Phase 1).

claims.claim: 'Terminal in a Garden' was BIAL's lead brief, chosen as a tribute to Bengaluru's 'Garden City of India' identity. It is the first of four design principles: Terminal in a Garden, Sustainability, Technology, and Art & Culture.
claims.detail: BIAL MD and CEO Hari Marar: 'Bengaluru has always been known as the Garden City of India ... an experience that feels like a stroll in a park. This is how the idea of Terminal in a Garden became the most important of the four design principles.' Dezeen reports that the client proposed the concept. Architectural Record explains the nickname: Bangalore was called the Garden City before it became a tech centre, because of its many public parks and temperate climate at about 3,000 ft altitude. Interior Design links the plan to the 20th-century garden-city movement in Bengaluru's planning.
claims.design_takeaway: ZMI's Bengaluru DNA should be a principle, not an ornament: nature present at every processing step, from kerb to gate, as in BLR.

claims.claim: Plants hang from the bamboo ceiling in two kinds of planter: bell-shaped 'bells' and chains of basket-like 'veils'. AJSK designed them, inspired by local bronze bells, and BIAL describes them as inspired by Karnataka's temples and homes. They start under the deep eaves at the kerbside drop-off and continue through the building. They cluster most densely in busy areas, so they also guide passengers.
claims.detail: BIAL counts about 500 bell and veil systems, each holding hundreds of plants. Architectural Record says the hanging baskets recall Ruth Asawa's sculptures. SOM's 2019 release puts the planted bells at entrance, check-in and security. The plants grow in soil-less media. The News Minute calls them 'bronze veils and bells', but whether they are actually bronze is unconfirmed. Separately, bell-shaped light fittings are made of banana-fibre paper with motifs inspired by Kasuti (Karnataka embroidery).
claims.design_takeaway: The hanging bell is BLR's single most recognisable element. In ZMI it can be the shared ceiling object. Its density can do the wayfinding job it does at BLR: tight clusters over the main paths, sparse elsewhere. That could be modelled as a crowd-flow cue in the game.

sources.quote: 500 such systems, each holding hundreds of plants (paraphrase of fetched text)

claims.claim: BIAL's landscape team sourced plants from many Indian habitats: more than 3,600 species, 620 endemic plants, 150 palm species, 7,700 transplanted trees, 100 varieties of lily, 96 lotus species, and 180 rare, endangered or threatened species. They were chosen partly for their water needs.
claims.detail: Figures are from BIAL's head of landscape, Prasanna Murthy, quoted by Civil Society (Jan 2023) and The News Minute (Nov 2022), and repeated by Airport Technology. Grant Associates adds 600-800-year-old trees and says over 7,700 existing trees and palms were saved and re-used (that last point is from a search snippet of their page). International Airport Review says the forest belt holds 2,000+ species of Indian flora. Visitors named orchids, anthuriums, lilies and lotus. I found no published species list for the hanging planters. Interior Design mentions 'centuries-old olive trees', which is unverified and odd for Bengaluru.
claims.design_takeaway: Plants in ZMI's Bengaluru sector should be named Indian natives (lotus and lily ponds, palms, orchids), not generic tropical greenery. Lotus ponds are an easy, recognisable 3D detail.

sources.quote: 600-800-year-old trees meet with over 180 rare, endangered and threatened species

claims.claim: The planting is watered by an automated, weather-based irrigation system that uses rainwater harvested on site. The airport has six rainwater-fed ponds holding 413 million litres.
claims.detail: International Airport Review (BIAL author): weather stations measure five parameters to set each day's irrigation, and drip emitters deliver 1-2.3 L per hour. Sensors monitor the health of the green walls. SOM's 2019 release describes a lagoon that collects rainwater for greywater reuse (cooling and irrigation), and an outdoor garden that doubles as a nursery for the terminal's plants. Architectural Record says rainwater from the roofs and site is captured, treated and reused for indoor and outdoor planting.
claims.design_takeaway: A ZMI 'water' system (rain to pond to drip irrigation to cooling) could appear in the game as a resource layer, with the Bengaluru lagoon as its visible landmark.

claims.claim: A planted 'forest belt' separates the landside processor building (check-in and security) from the gate piers. It is about 90 m wide and passengers cross it on covered bridges. It holds native planting, winding paths at several levels, and two-storey pavilions inspired by traditional cane weaving.
claims.detail: Sources disagree sharply on its area. Architectural Record gives 250,000 sq ft (about 23,200 m²) and Passenger Terminal Today gives 24,000 m², which agree with each other. Grant Associates gives 7 ha (70,000 m²), which probably includes surrounding landscape. Interior Design puts the pavilion landscape at 'nearly 3 acres' (about 1.2 ha). Width: 90 m (SOM). SOM calls the bridges 'covered, open-air'; Architectural Record calls them 'enclosed'. Pavilion material also differs: SOM calls them 'clad in bamboo', while Interior Design (Aug 2024) says Enter Projects Asia built five rattan pavilions, hand-woven in Bangkok over aluminium tubing, from 168 modules and about 5.5 miles of rattan. The pavilions hold retail, a Wolfgang Puck restaurant and lounges. SOM's Derek Moore mentioned planned 'tree houses' about 40 m tall on the landside. Their status is unconfirmed.
claims.design_takeaway: The forest belt is the strongest spatial idea to merge into ZMI: a planted band between processor and piers, crossed by bridges. In plan it makes a natural 'Bengaluru zone' between the Ahmedabad- and Mumbai-derived elements.

claims.claim: The ceiling is a lattice of cross-laid engineered bamboo layers that filters light from the skylights. Engineered bamboo also clads the columns and the roof soffits. It was treated against fire and insects and was SOM's first use of engineered bamboo.
claims.detail: BIAL's COO Satyaki Raghunath said the re-engineered bamboo was 'designed in India but mass-fabricated in China'. That conflicts with SOM's line that the roof is 'made entirely of domestically produced materials'; SOM may mean the roof structure rather than its bamboo finish. Airport Technology names Moso International (Netherlands) as bamboo supplier for ceilings and pillars, indoors and out. International Airport Review calls it 'engineered fire-retardant bamboo, used for the first time in India'. Lefkovits (SOM) cited bamboo's renewability and stiffness, which 'reduces the amount of secondary support required'. Rationale given by BIAL: bamboo is rapidly renewable, captures the 'Deccan Plateau's organic, earthy aesthetic', and echoes Indian cane weaving.
claims.design_takeaway: The bamboo lattice ceiling is the Bengaluru 'roofscape' gene. In a merged ZMI roof it can line the soffit under a different structural form (for example Mumbai-style), giving warmth and filtered light. Note that the bamboo is a finish over steel, not the load-bearing structure.

claims.claim: No reliable figure exists for how much bamboo T2 uses. One BIAL-authored article says 'over 923km of bamboo cladding'. The unit and basis of that number are unclear.
claims.detail: Neither SOM, Architectural Record nor Grant Associates gives a bamboo area or length. The 923 km could be total linear metres of laminated battens (possible for a lattice ceiling over about 100,000+ m²), but this is unconfirmed. I found no m² figure from the supplier (Moso) or SOM.
claims.design_takeaway: Don't quote a bamboo quantity in ZMI documents. If needed, attribute '923 km' to BIAL and call it linear length.

claims.claim: Over the check-in and retail halls, the roof is carried by long-span steel moment frames on an 18 m (59 ft) column grid. Each column is a cluster of four steel posts clad in bamboo. Over the gates, long-span steel trusses push the columns to the edges. The lower floors use a reinforced-concrete moment frame. SOM calls the roof one of the lightest large-scale terminal roofs in the world.
claims.detail: The roof is orthogonal and modular, designed for structural efficiency and future change. The four-post bamboo columns 'carry the texture of the lattices down to the floor' (Passenger Terminal Today). Kalzip (Germany) supplied the roof profiles and Geotrix the curtain wall. Architectural Record notes that much of the SOM team had worked on Mumbai CSMIA T2 (opened 2014), and contrasts Mumbai's 'enormous undulating roof' with Bengaluru's 'more orthogonal approach'.
claims.design_takeaway: Key merger insight: the same SOM team drew Mumbai's sculptural roof and Bengaluru's orthogonal bamboo grid. ZMI can combine Mumbai's undulating long-span roof with Bengaluru's 18 m bamboo-clad four-post column clusters and lattice soffit. In the 3D phase, an 18 m grid is an easy module.

sources.title: Architectural Record (9 Jan 2024)
sources.quote: Much of the SOM team had previously worked on a new terminal at Chhatrapati Shivaji International Airport in Mumbai that opened in 2014 ... the terminal in Bengaluru takes a more orthogonal approach ... one of the lightest large-scale terminal roofs in the world, according to the architects ... steel columns set on a 59-foot (18-meter) grid. Each column brings together a cluster of four steel posts clad in bamboo

sources.title: Passenger Terminal Today
sources.quote: Each of the building's columns comprises a cluster of four bamboo-clad steel members that have been designed to carry the texture of the lattices down to the floor

claims.claim: Daylight comes from extensive skylights over the main public spaces, filtered through the bamboo lattice, and from large perimeter curtain walls. Deep roof eaves shade much of the glazing. BIAL says the gardens and forest belt keep a microclimate 2-3 °C cooler than the surroundings.
claims.detail: SOM's 2019 release mentions high-performance glazing and shading. Indoor waterfalls are credited with cooling the interior. The 2-3 °C figure comes from BIAL's head of landscape (The News Minute, Moodie Davitt, Grant Associates). It is an operator claim, not independently measured. BIAL's COO says the skylights also feed the indoor plants and leave room to add more planting later.
claims.design_takeaway: Nagpur is much hotter than Bengaluru (Bengaluru sits at about 900 m). ZMI should keep BLR's deep eaves and filtered skylights but would need stronger shading, and should not assume BLR's mild-climate indoor-outdoor openness works unchanged. That is a genuine design tension to flag.

claims.claim: T2 has indoor waterfalls in the retail area, which BIAL says were inspired by Karnataka's waterways. Architectural Record describes them as red-stone walls with water running down them. SOM's original design paired the large indoor garden with rammed-earth walls, and outside there is a lagoon and lotus and lily ponds.
claims.detail: SOM 2019: a large indoor garden with rammed-earth walls and waterfalls leads to retail, with trees, small gardens and ponds inside and an outdoor garden around a lagoon. ACI/BIAL repeated the 'rammed-earth walls and waterfalls' wording in Dec 2023. SOM's 2024 release: 'the indoor waterfalls cool the interior environment.' Architectural Record: 'red-stone walls with water trickling down them in the retail area'. 'Rammed-earth' (2019 design) and 'red-stone' (2024 review) may describe the same as-built walls differently.
claims.design_takeaway: An earth-toned wall with a water cascade is a cheap, recognisable Bengaluru set piece for ZMI's airside retail zone, and works as a 3D landmark.

claims.claim: The finishes are warm, natural and largely local: engineered bamboo, locally sourced ivory-brown granite, umber-red brick (made locally by L&T), and furniture clad in traditionally woven rattan. The 2019 design specified natural terrazzo floors.
claims.detail: SOM 2019 lists brick walls, natural terrazzo floors and an engineered bamboo ceiling. Architectural Record (2024) lists local granite floors, interior brick 'L&T (locally made)', rattan millwork by Sreeji and Rachana Art, and custom gate-lounge lights by Rachana Art and Regent. BIAL's COO: 'locally available brick for external cladding'. Floors may be a mix of granite and terrazzo, which no source resolves.
claims.design_takeaway: For ZMI's Bengaluru material swatch: bamboo (honey), brick (umber-red), granite (ivory-brown), rattan (straw), plus planting green. This palette is easy to turn into game colours.

claims.claim: T2's art programme is themed on 'Naurasa', the nine emotions (rasas) of Bharata's Natyashastra. It has 60 works by 43 artists, chosen from more than 300 open-call entries. BLR Airport's in-house art team curated it under Yamini Telkar, Head of Art Programme, focusing on Karnataka's art forms first and other South Indian forms second.
claims.detail: The nine emotions: joy, fear, anger, love, courage, sadness, amazement, disgust and calm. Works include LN Tallur's 'In The Journey Of Naurasa' (nine birds around a Garuda-like winged figure), Krishnaraj Chonat's copper sculpture 'Gaatha', MA Rauf's Bidri installation, Anupama Hoskere's wooden puppets near the gates, Siddharth Kaneria's 'Cosmos' (glass panels with thali prints), and 'The Bamboo Story' at the entrance. In 2022 BIAL also opened a call for a monumental (about 20 m) sculpture for the forest belt (search snippet). Its outcome is unverified. I found no named external curator.
claims.design_takeaway: ZMI could run its own art programme with one shared theme across three regional sections, for example Naurasa (Bengaluru) alongside Mumbai's Jaya He programme and Ahmedabad crafts. A Bidri metal-inlay panel is a strong, specific Karnataka craft reference.

claims.claim: Before opening, the US Green Building Council pre-certified T2 as LEED Platinum (BD+C: New Construction), which SOM and BIAL describe as the largest terminal in the world with that pre-certification. T2 also holds Indian Green Building Council (IGBC) Platinum under the Green New Building rating.

Interior Design (Aug 2024) and a GBD Magazine search snippet instead say 'LEED Gold'. I could not resolve whether final LEED certification was Platinum or Gold. Platinum pre-certification and IGBC Platinum are well sourced.
claims.design_takeaway: For ZMI, cite 'LEED Platinum pre-certified + IGBC Platinum' for KIA T2, not 'LEED Platinum certified'.

claims.claim: BIAL says the BLR campus has run on 100% renewable electricity since 2023, about 70% solar and 30% wind, from rooftop solar plus an off-site solar-wind plant connected through the grid. It credits T2's solar panels and daylight harvesting with 24.9% energy savings.
claims.detail: BIAL COO Raghunath said the solar-wind plant is about three hours from the airport and that rooftop solar was being added to T2. Architectural Record: 'mostly solar, supplied by on-site and off-site arrays.' BIAL's own article calls the airport 'water-positive, energy-positive and carbon-neutral'. These are operator claims, not independently audited.
claims.design_takeaway: ZMI's energy story could combine Mumbai/Ahmedabad scale with a BLR-style renewable power purchase. In the game, a 'renewable share' metric is grounded in what BLR actually does.

claims.claim: In the 2023 Prix Versailles world titles (announced December 2023), KIA T2 won the Airports category's Special Prize for an Interior. It did not win the overall Airports title, which went to Aedas's Shenzhen Bao'an Satellite Concourse. The Exterior prize went to Grimshaw's Newark Terminal A.
claims.detail: BIAL publicised this as 'UNESCO's recognition as one of the World's Most Beautiful Airports'. Prix Versailles is an independent award acknowledged by UNESCO, with world titles announced at UNESCO headquarters in Paris. It is not a UNESCO award itself, so 'UNESCO award' is loose wording. 'World's most beautiful airports' refers to being on the Prix Versailles World Selection list. The 2023 jury was chaired by Elie Saab. Other awards: Best in Competition, 2024 AIANY + ASLA-NY Transportation + Infrastructure Design Excellence Awards (announced 15 Apr 2024). SOM also lists Dezeen Awards 2024, Architizer A+ 2024, Fast Company Innovation by Design 2024, ARCHITECT Architecture & Interiors 2024, and Interior Design Best of Year 2024. Grant Associates was a WAF 2024 finalist ('Inside: Public Buildings', search snippet only).
claims.design_takeaway: Precise wording for ZMI documents: 'Prix Versailles 2023 Special Prize for an Interior (Airports)'. The prize was for the interior (bamboo lattice and planting), which supports carrying the interior, not the massing, into ZMI.

claims.claim: The features press coverage most often singles out in T2: the honey-coloured bamboo lattice ceiling and four-post bamboo columns, plant-filled hanging bells and veils, the 10 m green wall, the forest belt with its bridges and woven pavilions, the waterfalls in retail, and the Naurasa art. Outside, a 108-ft statue of Kempegowda (Bengaluru's 16th-century founder, the airport's namesake) stands on the airport campus.
claims.detail: The statue was unveiled by PM Modi on 11 Nov 2022, the same day T2 opened (The News Minute). The list draws on what multiple outlets single out, not a passenger survey. Architectural Record sums up the experience as 'Relax, go outside, enjoy a bit of nature', in contrast to the usual speed-focused terminal. T1 (2008) shares none of these features. 'Recognisable Bengaluru airport' now means T2.
claims.design_takeaway: For ZMI's Bengaluru DNA, a minimum recognisable kit: (1) bamboo lattice soffit, (2) planted hanging bells, (3) a planted band crossed by bridges between processor and piers, (4) an earth-wall waterfall, (5) Naurasa-themed art. A returning Bengaluru passenger would probably recognise items 1-3 first.

open_questions: Final LEED level: SOM and BIAL report LEED Platinum pre-certification, while Interior Design (2024) and GBD Magazine say LEED Gold. Was a final certification ever issued, and at what level? The USGBC project directory would settle it.

Forest belt area: 23,200-24,000 m² (Architectural Record, Passenger Terminal Today) vs 7 ha (Grant Associates) vs about 3 acres for the pavilion landscape (Interior Design). Which boundary does each figure use?

Forest belt pavilion material: SOM calls them 'clad in bamboo', while Interior Design says Enter Projects Asia made them of hand-woven rattan over aluminium, in Bangkok. Possibly both (bamboo structure, rattan skin)?

Bamboo origin: BIAL's COO says it was mass-fabricated in China (Moso International as supplier), while SOM says the roof is 'made entirely of domestically produced materials'. Was only the roof structure domestic? Total bamboo quantity (the '923 km' figure) is also unverified.
Gate count: 11 new gates, 13 wide-body/28 narrow-body, or 22 contact plus 15 bus gates, depending on source. These need an authoritative BIAL stand list.
Phase 2 of T2: Moore says it adds 10 mppa, Marar says it goes from 25 to 45 mppa, and SOM's page says 50 mppa. Construction status as of Oct 2026 was not confirmed.
No published species list for the hanging bells and veils, and whether they are actually bronze or bronze-coloured is unconfirmed.
Were the 'rammed-earth walls' of the 2019 design built as such, or replaced by the 'red-stone walls' Architectural Record describes?
Outcome of BIAL's 2022 open call for a monumental (about 20 m) forest-belt sculpture was not verified.

verdicts.corrected_claim: T2 was designed by the New York office of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) for Bangalore International Airport Limited (BIAL). Grant Associates (UK) did the landscape architecture. Fashion designers Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla (AJSK) are credited with interior design; they also helped with the rattan furnishings and the planter design. Larsen & Toubro was general contractor and Arup did MEP/F engineering for T2. SOM did the structural engineering itself.
verdicts.note: I read the Architectural Record credits block myself. It lists SOM (New York office): design partners Roger Duffy and Colin Koop, managing partner Laura Ettelman, design principals Lefkovits and Moore. Structural engineers are SOM's Biswas, Besjak, Petrov, Jordan and King. Arup did m/e/p/f for T2 and Buro Happold for the transit hub. Other consultants: STUP (landside infrastructure), BNP (baggage) and Ch2m Hill (airside facilities). General contractor: L&T. Airport Technology confirms the Rs30.36bn (US$413m) L&T contract, awarded October 2018. One nuance: AR's text says AJSK 'assisted with furnishings' and 'helped with the design of planters', so it was a collaboration, not sole authorship. Airport Technology also names Turner Construction as project manager, which the researcher omitted.

sources.quote: Engineers: Skidmore, Owings & Merrill — Preetam Biswas, Charles Besjak... (structural); Arup (m/e/p/f for Terminal 2); Buro Happold (m/e/p/f for multimodal transit hub)

sources.title: Architectural Record (opened)
sources.quote: Fashion designers Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla assisted with furnishings ... and helped with the design of planters

sources.title: Airport Technology (opened)
sources.quote: BIAL awarded a Rs30.36bn ($413m) contract to L&T's Buildings & Factories business for the T2 construction in October 2018.

verdicts.corrected_claim: SOM's design was unveiled on 2 April 2019 with a first-phase target of March 2021. Construction began in 2019 (Airport Technology). PM Narendra Modi inaugurated T2 on 11 November 2022. Domestic operations began on Sunday 15 January 2023, with Star Air as the only airline that day. International operations began on 12 September 2023. BIAL had cancelled the planned 31 August 2023 switch on 30 August, at the final preparedness review.
verdicts.note: Every element checks out. The SOM release is dated 02 Apr 2019 and says the first phase was 'scheduled to be completed by March 2021'. The News Minute confirms the 11 Nov 2022 inauguration, and its 11 Jan 2023 piece confirms the 15 Jan date and Star Air. The ACI/BIAL release confirms 12 Sep 2023: SV866 from Jeddah at 10:15 and IndiGo 6E1167 to Colombo, with T2 then taking all international flights plus domestic AirAsia, Air India, Star Air and Vistara. Business Today (30 Aug 2023) confirms the 31 Aug postponement. AirAsia India announced on 3 Feb 2023 that it would move all domestic operations to T2 from 15 Feb 2023. Architectural Record gives completion as September 2023; SOM's project page says 'Construction Complete, Completion Year 2023, Design Finish Year 2018'. The 2019 construction start rests on Airport Technology alone, and the L&T contract dates from Oct 2018.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Phase 1 of T2 is about 255,000 m² over four levels; BIAL gives 255,661 m². A separate multimodal transit hub of about 123,000 m² (AR: 1.3 million sq ft) adjoins it. Together they come to roughly 380,000 m² (AR: 4.1 million sq ft).
verdicts.note: SOM's project page lists 'Building Gross Area: 380,000 square meters', with the terminal at 255,000 m² and the transit hub at 123,000 m². AR gives the terminal as 2.75 million sq ft, the hub as 1.3 million sq ft and the total as 4.1 million sq ft including the hub. AR also says a further 'extension to the south of the new terminal' (Phase 2) was 'still on the drawing board'. Airport Technology gives 255,661 m² over four levels. Grant Associates gives 255,645 m² but describes it as 'the airport's expansion, executed in two phases', which is ambiguous.

verdicts.corrected_claim: T2 Phase 1 has a design capacity of 25 mppa. SOM's Derek Moore says about 20 mppa of that is international. Most sources say Phase 2 adds about 20 mppa, taking T2 to about 45 mppa; these are the Passenger Terminal Today text, BIAL CEO Hari Marar, L&T and SOM's project page. Moore's quote that the second phase adds 10 mppa is the outlier. The whole airport handled 41.88 million passengers in FY2024-25 and 44.47 million in FY2025-26 (37.24m domestic, 7.23m international).
verdicts.note: The Passenger Terminal Today article contradicts itself. Moore is quoted saying 'The second phase would add another 10 mppa', but the article's own text says 'A subsequent phase will add a further 200,000m2 and 20 million in annual capacity'. L&T's blog also says 'Phase 2 adding 20 million more'. Marar in The Week (22 May 2023) gives 45 million for T2 and 'nearly 80 million' total. That makes +20 the majority figure. verdicts.corrected_claim: The features press coverage most often singles out in T2 are: the honey-coloured bamboo lattice ceiling and four-post bamboo columns, the plant-filled hanging bells and veils, the green walls, the forest belt with its bridges and pavilions, the waterfalls in retail, and the Naurasa art. Outside, a 108 ft statue of Kempegowda, Bengaluru's 16th-century founder and the airport's namesake, stands on the airport premises; PM Modi unveiled it on 11 Nov 2022, the day T2 was inaugurated.
verdicts.note: The factual parts are confirmed. The News Minute (11 Nov 2022) says Modi 'also unveiled the 108-foot-tall KempeGowda statue built on the premises', the same day he inaugurated T2. Dezeen and AR describe the bamboo grid, the 90 m forest belt and the planting, and AR ends with 'Relax, go outside, enjoy a bit of nature.' I could only source the founder description (Kempe Gowda, 1510-1569) to Wikipedia; The Hindu and Indian Express were not fetchable. The 'most often singled out' ranking is editorial interpretation, not a measured fact.

research.topic: Ahmedabad: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Airport (SVPIA, AMD) and the Ahmedabad / Gujarat architectural heritage a merged ZMI hub could reference

claims.claim: SVPIA's current international terminal (T2) opened in July 2010. Union Civil Aviation Minister of State Praful Patel inaugurated it, at a reported project cost of about Rs 290 crore. Terminal 1 is the older domestic building. None of the sources found names an architect, and none describes the terminal as a design project of note.
claims.detail: Cost figures: Rs 290 crore (narendramodi.in report, seen as a search snippet; the page itself timed out), Rs 290.92 crore (Lok Sabha answer, seen only as a search-tool summary; the PDF was unreachable), Rs 291 crore (trade press). A 2011 DeshGujarat article confirms Praful Patel 'opened a newly constructed international terminal' the year before. An older airport-technology.com profile gives T2 as 7,825 m2 with 23 check-in counters, but that figure is out of date (see amd-02). Wikipedia-derived pages give 5 July 2010 for the inauguration and 15 September 2010 for the start of international operations. They also say the design 'followed Singapore Changi', which is unverified. Several searches (AAI records, trade press, Adani job listings) found no named architect or design concept for T1 or T2. The terminal's distinctiveness comes from interior art added later (amd-05, amd-06), not from its architecture. Airport history from travel sites (opened 1937, international status 23 May 2000, renaming in 1991, 1992 or 2005 depending on the site) is low quality and unverified.
claims.design_takeaway: Do not cite SVPIA's building form as DNA. It is a generic glass-and-steel box with no attributed architect. Ahmedabad's contribution to ZMI should come from the city (jaali, stepwell, pol, kite, Patel) and from the operator's own 'Amaru Amdavad' interior vocabulary, not from SVPIA's structure. Saying this openly in the design document makes it more credible.
