claims.claim: By March 2026, T2 had a 49,000 m2 built-up area with 52 check-in counters, 17 departure and 22 arrival immigration counters and 8 Fast Track Immigration e-gates. From 29 March 2026, Air India moved all of its domestic flights (210 weekly) from T1 to T2.
claims.detail: T2 has been extended in steps: a 2,550 m2 arrival block (Aug 2023), a 2,100 m2 departure/check-in extension with 20 more counters (Oct 2024), and an 'extended check-in hall' (FY25, per the Adani May 2025 media note). Inter-terminal electric shuttle buses link T1 and T2. Terminal numbering is inconsistent across sources (a 'T3' for Hajj/secondary traffic is also mentioned).
claims.design_takeaway: AMD is now a two-terminal airport that keeps expanding piecemeal. In the game, an 'AMD pier' can be modelled as one where domestic and international share a single building, which matches where SVPIA itself is heading (amd-08).

sources.title: DeshGujarat, 27 Mar 2026: Air India to move all domestic flight operations to Terminal 2
sources.quote: Opened: 'Spread across a 49,000 sq. m built-up area' ... '52 check-in counters' ... 'From 29 March onwards, all Air India arrivals and departures will operate exclusively from Terminal 2.'

sources.title: DeshGujarat, 26 Oct 2024: Ahmedabad Airport opens expanded departure space in terminal 2
sources.quote: Opened: 'The upgraded 2,100 sq m area offers 20 additional check-in counters' plus a 'wall mural depicting places of Ahmedabad'.

claims.claim: Adani Ahmedabad International Airport Ltd took over SVPIA from the Airports Authority of India at midnight on 6/7 November 2020. It holds a 50-year lease covering operations, management and development. AAI keeps customs, immigration, quarantine and security.
claims.detail: Adani won the leases for six AAI airports (Ahmedabad, Lucknow, Jaipur, Mangaluru, Thiruvananthapuram, Guwahati) in February 2019. Business Today dates the start of commercial operations to Sunday 8 Nov 2020, while The Week (7 Nov 2020) reports the key handover at midnight. Some secondary sites wrongly give 2021. The current operator entity is called Ahmedabad International Airport Ltd (AIAL), under Adani Airport Holdings Ltd.
claims.design_takeaway: In the ZMI story, the 'closing' of AMD means retiring an Adani-run concession. If the narrative mentions the operator, keep it neutral. The handover-of-the-key ceremony could become a game narrative beat ('handing over the key' of each old airport to ZMI).

sources.title: The Week, 7 Nov 2020: Adani Group takes over Ahmedabad Airport operations
sources.quote: Opened: 'At midnight tonight, the ceremonial Handing Over of the Key to AAIAL will mark the new chapter for Ahmedabad Airport' ... operations, management and development 'for a period of 50 years.'

sources.title: Business Today, 8 Nov 2020: Adani Group takes over Ahmedabad airport on lease for 50 years
sources.quote: Search snippet: the group 'took over Ahmedabad airport on Sunday and has started commercial operations'.

claims.claim: SVPIA handled 13,427,697 passengers in FY2024-25 (1 Apr 2024 to 31 Mar 2025), up 14.8% from 11,696,227. That was over 11 million domestic and over 2.2 million international passengers, with 101,119 aircraft movements. Its record day was 25 January 2025: 48,137 passengers and 351 movements.
claims.detail: The same note gives about 36,800 passengers and 288 flights per day, to 48 domestic and 16 international destinations. A DeshGujarat report (Aug 2025) rounds FY25 to '1.2 crore', which conflicts with the operator's 1.34 crore. The 1.22 crore figure is an April-February partial-year number. Use the operator figure.
claims.design_takeaway: AMD's real traffic, about 13.4 M pax/yr, is small next to BOM and BLR. In the merger it is a minor contributor by volume but a major one by identity. Weight its design DNA more heavily than its traffic share.

sources.title: Adani / SVPIA media note, 13 May 2025: Ahmedabad Airport's Transformation Takes Flight
sources.quote: Opened (PDF text): 'SVPI Airport welcomed an unprecedented 13,427,697 passengers, marking a substantial 14.8% increase compared to the 11,696,227 travellers' ... 'highest-ever ... on 25 January 2025, serving an impressive 48,137 passengers with 351 aircraft movements.'

claims.claim: In August 2023 the operator opened a 2,550 m2 international arrival block in T2 with 24 immigration counters (up from 16). Its stated design theme is 'Amaru Amdavad' (My Amdavad), and it explicitly refers to Ahmedabad being the 'first world heritage city'. Features include 'shimmering torans' overhead and planned 'Aangan Van' planters with motifs drawn from the Dholavira script.
claims.detail: The press release says the planters will form 'a sky-lit indoor oasis'. Aangan = courtyard and van = grove, which echoes the pol-house courtyard. The planters and art were described as 'ongoing' or 'will be added soon', so whether they were completed is unconfirmed. The arrivals hall also has six baggage belts.
claims.design_takeaway: This is the operator's own recognisability vocabulary for AMD: toran (festive gateway garland), courtyard (aangan), the heritage-city claim, and Harappan (Dholavira) script. ZMI can take the toran as the formal 'welcome arch' over the AMD-derived arrivals route, and the aangan as a sky-lit courtyard garden. A returning AMD passenger would already link these to 'home'.

sources.title: Adani Airports media release, 24 Aug 2023: All new arrival area in the international terminal of Ahmedabad Airport
sources.quote: Opened (PDF text): 'The new arrival block spanning 2550 sqm ... boasts 24 state-of-the-art immigration counters' ... 'Ahmedabad being the first world heritage city' ... 'fitting theme of "Amaru Amdavad" (My Amdavad)' ... 'pass beneath an array of shimmering torans' ... '"Aangan Van" planters ... through Dholavira encryption'.

claims.claim: SVPIA expresses local identity mainly through art installations. Examples: 'Wave of Life', a fabric kite installation about 150 m long across the airport facade for the 2022 kite season (Idea Factor). Carved Gujarati wooden panels at T2. A haveli-style carved wooden arch at T1. Kutch embroidered textiles. In September 2025, T2 added a 350 m metallic mural with jaali-style illustrations ('Conversations of Freedom', on Gandhi and Sardar Patel), a 'Utsav Wall' for Navratri and Uttarayan, and 'Pragati-ni-Patang', bronze children with illuminated acrylic kites.
claims.detail: The 2022 items come from an AviationPros press release dated 12 Jan 2022. The September 2025 items come from a single travel-site article (IndianEagle, 17 Sep 2025), corroborated only by a News Arena tag page that dates the unveiling to 16 Sep 2025. No official operator statement was found, so the 350 m figure rests on one source. No source links any SVPIA jaali artwork specifically to the Sidi Saiyyed window. Another listed work is a 'Hulchul Wall' showing Ahmedabad's pols and facades.
claims.design_takeaway: The existing airport already uses kites, jaali, haveli wood carving and Patel as its identity markers. ZMI can promote these from decoration to architecture: a kite-canopy roof, a jaali facade, a timber-carved gate. That turns them into structure instead of murals.

sources.title: AviationPros press release, 12 Jan 2022: Ahmedabad's Airport Reflects Cultural Heritage with Local Flavor
sources.quote: Opened: 'Wave of Life' fabric kite installation by Idea Factor, 'approx. 150 m long', across the facade; carved wooden panels at T2; wooden arch at T1 based on 18th-19th century Gujarat havelis.

sources.title: IndianEagle, 17 Sep 2025: Art installations at Ahmedabad airport
sources.quote: Opened: 'Conversations of Freedom' ... a 350-metre mural in metallic sheets with jaali-style illustrations; 'Utsav Wall – Navratri and Uttarayan'; 'Pragati-ni-Patang' with illuminated acrylic kites.

claims.claim: An 18 ft statue of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel by sculptor Ram Sutar was dedicated at SVPIA on 9 January 2011. AAI paid Rs 50 lakh for it, and it was described as possibly the tallest statue of Patel in Gujarat at the time.
claims.detail: Its exact position (forecourt or which terminal) is not stated in the source. Ram Sutar later became known as the sculptor associated with the Statue of Unity, but no source opened here confirms that link, so it is not claimed.
claims.design_takeaway: Regular AMD passengers know the Patel statue. ZMI could move it, or a cast of it, to the landside forecourt or the 'Ekta' (unity) hall as a literal carry-over. It is a cheap and emotionally strong DNA transfer.

sources.title: DeshGujarat, 8-9 Jan 2011: Sardar Patel statue at Ahmedabad airport
sources.quote: Opened: 18 ft, 'possibly the tallest statue of Shri Sardar Patel in entire Gujarat'; made by Padma award artist Ram Sutar; 'The Airport Authority of India has spent Rs. 50 lakh in making and installing this statue.'

claims.claim: Adani is building a New Integrated Terminal Building (NITB) at SVPIA. It will combine domestic and international operations, and phase 1 costs over Rs 3,000-3,100 crore. Construction began by July 2026 next to the existing domestic terminal on the vacated T3 side, with phase 1 targeted for 2029-30. No architect, design concept or rendering has been published.
claims.detail: DeshGujarat (7 Aug 2025): cost 'exceeding ₹3,100 crore'; construction expected 'by March 2026'; both phases before 2036; capacity rising from about 1.2 crore (FY25) to 2 crore passengers a year; 'over 10 aerobridges'; DigiYatra entrance-to-gate in 'as little as 12 minutes'; T1 to be demolished once the new terminal opens; ATC tower, state hangar and GA terminal to be relocated; linked to Ahmedabad's Olympic ambitions. Swarajya (29 Jul 2026): 'more than Rs 3,000 crore', construction commenced, 'T3 has nearly been vacated', no design details. Separately, Benoy says it produced three architectural concepts for an Executive Terminal/FBO at Ahmedabad, one of them vernacular with deep overhangs and local stone. That comes only from a search snippet (the project page did not load), so it is low confidence.
claims.design_takeaway: In ZMI's fiction, AMD closes just as its own integrated terminal is being built. The narrative can say ZMI 'absorbs' the NITB programme. Because no NITB design exists yet, ZMI's AMD-derived elements will not clash with a real published design.

sources.title: Swarajya, 29 Jul 2026: Ahmedabad airport begins construction of Rs 3,000-crore integrated terminal
sources.quote: Opened: first phase 'estimated to cost more than Rs 3,000 crore', targeted for 2029-30, built next to the existing domestic terminal on the T3 side; 'T3 has nearly been vacated'.

sources.title: DeshGujarat, 7 Aug 2025: Construction of New Integrated Terminal at Ahmedabad Airport to Kick Off by March 2026
sources.quote: Opened: 'exceeding ₹3,100 crore' ... 'over 10 aerobridges' ... entrance to gate 'in as little as 12 minutes' ... existing domestic terminal to be demolished.

sources.title: Benoy: Fixed Base / Executive Terminal (Ahmedabad)
sources.quote: Search snippet only (page content did not load): commissioned by Adani Airports to produce 'three distinct architectural concepts for a new Executive Terminal and FBO'; one vernacular with deep overhangs and local stone.

claims.claim: The 'Historic City of Ahmadabad', the walled city founded in 1411 by Sultan Ahmad Shah on the eastern bank of the Sabarmati, was inscribed on the World Heritage List on 8 July 2017 at the 41st session of the World Heritage Committee, under criteria (ii) and (v). The Government of India describes it as the first Indian city, and the third in Asia, to be inscribed.
claims.detail: The property covers 535.7 ha. It includes the remains of the city walls and gates, 28 historic buildings of national significance (Sultanate-era monuments), and the traditional urban fabric of pols and puras. A UNESCO record also cites 2,696 buildings protected by the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation. The 41st session was held in Kraków; that comes from a search-result summary, not a page opened here. The proposal had earlier been deferred. UNESCO and PIB pages returned 403 to direct fetch, so the UNESCO and PIB facts here come from search snippets. Gujarat Tourism, opened directly, confirms 'the first city in India to be inscribed' and the year 2017.
claims.design_takeaway: 'First World Heritage City' is the strongest single civic claim Ahmedabad has, and the operator already uses it (amd-05). ZMI's AMD zone can cite the walled city: a gate (darwaza) threshold into the AMD-derived concourse, and planning by gated, named neighbourhoods.

sources.title: PIB (Ministry of Culture): Declaration of Historic City of Ahmadabad as a UNESCO's World Heritage Property
sources.quote: Search snippet (403 on fetch): inscribed '8th July, 2017 during the 41st Session of World Heritage Committee' ... 'the first city in India and the third in Asia to be inscribed' ... 'Criteria (ii) and (v)'.

sources.title: UNESCO WHC: Historic City of Ahmadabad
sources.quote: Search snippet (403 on fetch): 'The walled city of Ahmadabad was founded by Sultan Ahmad Shah in 1411 AD on the eastern bank of the Sabarmati River.'

sources.title: Gujarat Tourism: Ahmedabad World Heritage City
sources.quote: Opened: 'the first city in India to be inscribed'; 'inscribed in UNESCO's World Heritage City list of 2017'.

claims.claim: The walled city is organised into pols (gated residential streets) entered through a khadki gate. A pol holds roughly 50-100 closely packed houses with shared side walls, plus community wells, chabutaro (raised bird feeders) and public and religious buildings. The houses are composite timber and brick-lime structures around a central courtyard, with their own rainwater storage. UNESCO calls the timber architecture the most distinctive aspect of the city's heritage.
claims.detail: Pol counts vary widely: Gujarat Tourism caption about 360; a heritage write-up 'roughly 600'; one magazine 6,000, which looks wrong. Treat the number as uncertain. The AMC Heritage Cell was set up in July 1996 with CRUTA Foundation, the first heritage cell in any Indian urban local body. It has restored 20+ chabutaras and has run a daily heritage walk since 1997. UNESCO monitoring flags neglected pol houses as a conservation concern. Chabutaro descriptions say they are raised on a post 'like trees', with grain storage at the base, kept high to protect birds from dogs.
claims.design_takeaway: The pol suggests a planning model for the AMD-derived pier: gated 'neighbourhood' gate-lounges around a shared court, each with a named gateway (khadki). A chabutaro-like vertical element (a carved post with lighting or a planter on top) can mark each pol-lounge. Carved timber brackets and jharokha balconies can line the mezzanine edge. The courtyard house with its own rain storage also connects to a stepwell-style water strategy.

sources.title: UNESCO WHC Urban Heritage Atlas: Historic City of Ahmedabad
sources.quote: Search snippet (403 on fetch): residential districts 'centred around a main street (pol) and accessed through a gate (khadki)'; 'between 50 and 100 closely packed houses'; public spaces with 'community wells, bird feeders (chabutaro) ... and richly decorated wooden residential buildings'; 'timber-based architecture ... is the most unique aspect of its heritage'.

sources.title: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation: Heritage Department
sources.quote: Search snippet: established with CRUTA Foundation 'in July 1996' as 'the first heritage cell in India within an Urban Local Body'; restored 'more than 20 old Chabutras'.

sources.title: AMC Heritage City: Dhal Ni Pol
sources.quote: Opened: lanes are 'tiny Khacho or khadki braching out, similar to the limbs of a tree'; chowks where 'the community often celebrates holidays like Holi and Garba'.

claims.claim: The Sidi Saiyyed mosque, completed around 1572/73 CE just before the Mughal conquest of Gujarat, is the last major Gujarat Sultanate monument. Its sandstone window screens (jalis) include the 'tree of life' window: a single palm with spreading fronds, wrapped by a flowering vine that emerges from the mouth of a makara. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation calls the jalis 'a symbol of the city of Ahmedabad'.
claims.detail: There are ten windows: three on the north side, three on the south, and four on the west wall either side of a blind central opening. That central opening was walled up, probably because the mosque was unfinished when the Mughals invaded. Per IIMA, the creeper pattern is the rati-kera, one of eleven Hindu/Buddhist creeper patterns, combined with Islamic arabesque. The patron, Sidi Saiyyed, was a Habshi (Abyssinian/African) noble in the Gujarat Sultanate army. He died on 24 Dec 1576 and is buried there. Completion date: 1573 (AMC) vs 'around 1572/73 CE' (IIMA).
claims.design_takeaway: This is Ahmedabad's emblem, and it fits a merger story: a carving by an African patron that blends Hindu iconography with Islamic arabesque. A tree-of-life jaali, abstracted rather than copied, makes a strong primary facade screen or gate-wall motif for ZMI. Parametric jaali also solves glare and heat on a central-India airside facade. Avoid copying the exact window, because IIM-A's logo is already a stylised version of it.

sources.title: IIMA Archives: The story of our logo (Prof. Vijaya Sherry Chand, IIMA Alumnus, Oct 2017)
sources.quote: Opened (PDF text): 'completed around 1572/73 CE ... the last major example of the Gujarat Sultanate style' ... 'There are ten windows' ... 'a single palm tree with the fronds spreading out at the top. And then there is a vine ... emerge from the mouth of a makara'.

sources.title: AMC Heritage City: Sidi Saiyyed Mosque
sources.quote: Opened: 'completed in 1573'; carvings 'hewn from solid stone'; jalis regarded as 'a symbol of the city of Ahmedabad'; tree-of-life design appears on the IIM Ahmedabad logo and on souvenirs.

claims.claim: IIM Ahmedabad's logo is based on one specific Sidi Saiyyed window: the one immediately north of the blind central opening on the west wall. Vikram Sarabhai and Kamla Chowdhry briefed the ad agency Lintas in late 1963 (team led by Hasan Taj). The IIMA Board adopted the first version on 1 July 1964, and the final version with the Sanskrit motto was settled by February 1967.
claims.detail: Some secondary sources say the logo was adopted in 1961; the IIMA archive contradicts this. Hasan Taj said the logo jali 'was not a replica' and that he replaced the original flowers with 'ever-dreaming and aspiring stars' (five on the right, four on the left). The motto is Vidyaviniyogaadvikasah, by Prof. H. N. Pathak. Chowdhry said Sarabhai chose the jali partly because the mosque sat at the city's centre, its 'marma'.
claims.design_takeaway: This precedent shows the jaali can be abstracted and still read clearly as Ahmedabad. ZMI should follow the same approach (reinterpret, do not replicate) and should check that its jaali motif does not look too much like the IIMA trademark.

sources.title: IIMA Archives: The story of our logo
sources.quote: Opened (PDF text): 'This brief was given in late 1963' ... 'The design proposed by Lintas was adopted in a Board meeting held on July 1, 1964' ... 'by February 1967, the logo that we have today was finalized' ... 'the jali, even though based on the Sidi Saiyad jali, was not a replica'.

claims.claim: Adalaj stepwell (Rudabai ni Vav), about 18 km north of Ahmedabad near Gandhinagar, carries a Sanskrit inscription dated Samvat 1555 (1498 or 1499 CE) naming Queen Rudadevi/Rudabai, wife of the Vaghela chief Virsimha (Veer Singh), as its builder. It was completed under Sultan Mahmud Begada. It is a five-storey trabeate sandstone structure about 75 m long. Three entrance stairs meet at an octagonal landing under an octagonal opening, and a stepped corridor then descends to the well.
claims.detail: Date: inscription Samvat 1555 converts to 1498 (Incredible India 'construction began in 1498', Studio Matrx) or 1499 (Archnet, Athens Journal). Gujarat Tourism's trip-planner says 'built by Mahmud Begada in 1411', which is almost certainly wrong: 1411 is the founding year of Ahmedabad. Length: 75.3 m (Athens Journal); the same paper elsewhere says '250 feet' (about 76 m). Entrances: the Athens Journal says south, west and east stairs with the long axis north-south; Studio Matrx's caption says north, south and east. That conflict is unresolved. The structure is post-and-beam with no arches. Carvings include the Kalpavriksha (tree of life), Ami Khumbor (pot of the water of life) and a Navagraha frieze. Incredible India: 'sunlight never touches the water directly except at noon'. The Rudabai sati and suicide legend is folklore and is not in the inscription.
claims.design_takeaway: Adalaj's section maps directly onto an airport: three landside entrances converge on one octagonal light-well 'landing' (a central security or orientation hall), then a single descending axis leads to the 'water' (the airside concourse or train station). Post-and-beam galleries stacked around light shafts give a clear model for a multi-level terminal atrium.

sources.title: Sriparvathy & Salahsha, 'Adalaj Stepwell: A Magical Resonance of Architectural Ingenuity', Athens Journal of Architecture 7(2), Apr 2021, pp. 275-304
sources.quote: Opened (PDF text): 'The five-storeyed structure is an octagonal polygon in plan ... 75.3 meters in length and is oriented along the North-South direction' ... 'commissioned in 1499 A.D. by Queen Rudabai'.

sources.title: Incredible India (Ministry of Tourism): Adalaj Stepwell
sources.quote: Opened: 'Construction began in 1498' ... 'a five-storied poem in stone' ... 'octagonal opening allows light and air to filter through' ... 'sunlight never touches the water directly except at noon.'

sources.title: Studio Matrx: Adalaj Stepwell
sources.quote: Opened: dated 1498 CE ('inscribed; high confidence'); 'five storeys of pillared galleries and landings'; carved sandstone, trabeate, 'no arches or vaults'.

claims.claim: Adalaj is widely described as about 5-6 °C cooler at its lower levels than at ground level. No published measurement backing that figure was found. The one peer-reviewed architectural paper located describes the cooling only qualitatively, attributing it to the thermal mass of stone and ground and to evaporation from the water body.
claims.detail: Figures in circulation: 'six degrees cooler' (Gujarat Tourism, hedged with 'it is said'), 5-6 °C (Studio Matrx, uncited), 6-8 °C (eSamskriti, uncited), 'nearly 5 °C' (blog, uncited). The Athens Journal paper (2021) says only 'As a person descends, the temperature keeps reducing'. Related research on Jodhpur stepwells (Cardiff University, ICUC12 2025; an ENVI-met CFD study) is underway but gave no figures in the snippets seen. This topic brief asked for a measured difference, and none could be verified.
claims.design_takeaway: In the design document, write 'traditionally reported as about 5-6 °C cooler (unmeasured)', not a hard number. The principle (sunken, shaded, thermally massive, evaporatively cooled) is still a valid passive-cooling argument for a sunken stepwell plaza or forecourt at ZMI in Nagpur's 45 °C+ summers.

sources.title: Gujarat Tourism trip planner: Adalaj Stepwell
sources.quote: Opened: 'the temperature inside the well is six degrees cooler than outside' (prefaced 'it is said'); also gives the erroneous date 'built by Mahmud Begada in 1411'.

'stone and the ground below acting as thermal buffers' ... 'Evaporative cooling'. No numeric measurement given.

claims.claim: Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen's Stepwell) at Patan, Gujarat, was built in the 11th century CE, traditionally dated 1063, by Queen Udayamati of the Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty as a memorial to King Bhimdev I. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014 (38th session, Doha, criteria (i) and (iv)). UNESCO describes it as 'an inverted temple highlighting the sanctity of water', divided into seven levels of stairs, with more than 500 principal and over 1,000 minor sculptures.
claims.detail: ASI: the fourth level is the deepest and leads to a rectangular tank of 9.5 x 9.4 m at 23 m depth. The well shaft at the west end is 10 m in diameter and 30 m deep. Property 4.68 ha, buffer 125.44 ha. Overall size about 64 x 20 m (secondary source only). After geotectonic changes and the shift of the Saraswati in the 13th century, it filled with silt, which preserved it. Cousens and Burgess saw it in the 1890s almost fully buried; ASI excavated and restored it from the 1940s to the 1980s (sources differ on dates). Gujarat Tourism says 'more than 800 sculptures', which differs from UNESCO's 500+ principal and 1,000+ minor. Inscription date reported as 22 June 2014. UNESCO pages returned 403, so the UNESCO wording is from search snippets.
claims.design_takeaway: 'Inverted temple' is a strong idea for a hub that sits at India's centre: descend to arrive. Seven levels of colonnaded pavilions stepping down to water gives a section for a central arrivals or rail interchange 'kund', with sculpture niches used for wayfinding art. Rani-ki-Vav is in Patan, not Ahmedabad; present it as Gujarat heritage that Ahmedabad passengers know, not as an Ahmedabad monument.

sources.title: UNESCO WHC: Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen's Stepwell) at Patan, Gujarat
sources.quote: Search snippet (403 on fetch): 'initially built as a memorial in the 11th century CE' ... 'designed as an inverted temple highlighting the sanctity of water' ... 'divided into seven levels of stairs' ... 'more than five hundred principle sculptures and over a thousand minor ones'.

sources.title: Archaeological Survey of India: Rani-ki-Vav, Patan
sources.quote: Search snippet (fetch returned only site chrome): fourth level 'leads into a rectangular tank of 9.5 by 9.4 metres, at a depth of 23 metres'; well shaft '10 metres in diameter and 30 metres deep'.

sources.title: Gujarat Tourism: Rani Ki Vav, Patan
sources.quote: Opened: 'built in 1063 by Rani Udayamati of the Chaulukya Dynasty' to commemorate Bhimdev I; 1890s visit found it 'completely buried under silt'; UNESCO since 2014.

claims.claim: The Reserve Bank of India's ₹100 note in the Mahatma Gandhi (New) Series, announced on 19 July 2018, has a lavender base colour and a Rani-ki-Vav motif on its reverse.
claims.detail: The note measures 66 x 142 mm. This comes from search snippets of RBI press releases and the RBI annual report table ('100 · Rani ki Vav · Lavender · 66 mm × 142 mm'), not from a page opened here.
claims.design_takeaway: Every Indian passenger, not only those from Ahmedabad, carries an image of Rani-ki-Vav in their wallet. That makes a stepwell motif recognisable nationally, which helps a hub meant to unite three cities.

sources.quote: Search snippet: Mahatma Gandhi (New) Series ₹100 note; 'motif of "RANI KI VAV" on the reverse'; base colour lavender; 66 mm x 142 mm.

claims.claim: Uttarayan (Makar Sankranti, 14 January) is Gujarat's kite festival. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation calls it 'a uniquely Gujarati phenomenon', when the skies over the state's cities fill with kites from before dawn until after dark and almost all normal activity stops as people fly kites from rooftops and roadways.
claims.detail: The AMC page gives no attendance figure, and no reliable count of participants in the city-wide rooftop festival was found. Hazards: PTI reports deaths every year from kite strings (manja) and falls from rooftops (date of that snippet unclear). Uttarayan is a citizen rooftop event, distinct from the official International Kite Festival (amd-18).
claims.design_takeaway: Kites are Ahmedabad's most joyful and most widely recognised image. Use them as a roof language (tensile 'kite' canopies or a sky of suspended kites in the AMD-derived hall) and as a seasonal game event on 14 January: a traffic surge, kite-string and bird-strike hazards near the runway, and a sky-lit hall. Also take note of the real bird-strike and string-hazard issue for airside operations.

sources.title: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation: Uttarayan Festival
sources.quote: Opened (via curl): 'The festival of Uttarayan is a uniquely Gujarati phenomenon, when the skies over most cities of the state fill with kites from before dawn until well after dark' ... 'almost all normal activity is shut down and everyone takes to the rooftops and roadways to fly kites'.

claims.claim: Ahmedabad has hosted an International Kite Festival as part of Uttarayan since 1989. The 2026 edition at the Sabarmati Riverfront was inaugurated on 12 January 2026 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. It had 135 international kite flyers from 50 countries, 65 from 13 Indian states and 871 from 16 Gujarat districts.
claims.detail: Figures come from a PTI report carried by Siasat. Incredible India lists the next edition as 10-14 January 2027 at the Sabarmati Riverfront. Earlier editions were smaller (e.g., a reported 256 flyers from 32 countries in 2009, from a secondary source, low confidence). A PTI line says the previous year drew 'more than 3.83 lakh visitors across Gujarat' (search-summary only).
claims.design_takeaway: The festival puts international visitors into Ahmedabad's sky every January, so it is a ready-made recurring event for ZMI's calendar and a reason for a seasonal arrivals 'kite gate' that changes each January.

sources.title: Siasat (PTI), 12 Jan 2026: International Kite Festival 2026

'135 international kite flyers representing 50 countries and 65 enthusiasts from 13 Indian states' ... 'Since 1989, Ahmedabad has hosted the International Kite Festival'.

sources.title: Incredible India: International Kite Festival
sources.quote: Opened: '10–14 January 2027' ... 'Sabarmati Riverfront, Ahmedabad'; 'Celebration of Uttarayan Tradition'.

claims.claim: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, led the States Department that integrated 'over 560 princely states' into the Union, covering nearly 40% of India's territory and population, around 1947. The Government calls him the 'Iron Man'. His birth anniversary, 31 October, has been observed as Rashtriya Ekta Diwas (National Unity Day) since 2014.
claims.detail: Count: PIB (Oct 2025) says 'over 560'. Gujarat Tourism says 'all 562'. Other secondary sources say 565. Use 'over 560' or '562 (commonly cited)'. The States Department was formed on 25 June 1947 under Patel, with V. P. Menon as Secretary (older PIB release, seen as a search snippet). Hyderabad, Junagadh and Jammu & Kashmir held out at first. 2025 was Patel's 150th birth anniversary. He also founded the All-India Services, the 'Steel Frame'.
claims.design_takeaway: Patel is the real-world figure for ZMI's core concept, merging many separate entities into one. AMD's namesake gives ZMI its founding story. A 'Hall of Unity' (Ekta Hall) where the three source cities' design elements meet works on both levels. 31 October could be a game event.

sources.title: PIB backgrounder, 30 Oct 2025: Rashtriya Ekta Diwas
sources.quote: Opened (PDF text): 'He was tasked with unifying over 560 princely states—covering nearly 40% of India's territory and population—into the Union of India' ... 'decisive leadership of this "Iron Man"' ... 'The day was first celebrated in 2014'.

sources.title: Gujarat Tourism: Statue of Unity
sources.quote: Search snippet: 'He was responsible for uniting all 562 princely states of the country to build the Republic of India.'

claims.claim: The Statue of Unity, a statue of Patel 182 m (597 ft) tall, stands on Sadhu Bet, a river island in the Narmada near Kevadia (now Ekta Nagar), Narmada district, Gujarat. It was consecrated and inaugurated on 31 October 2018 and is the world's tallest statue (Guinness World Records).
claims.detail: L&T, the builder, says it is clad with '6,500+ macro and micro bronze panels' on a concrete and steel superstructure and was 'built in just 33 months'. The client was Sardar Sarovar Narmada Nigam Ltd. A 300 m bridge links Sadhu Bet to the mainland (PIB, search snippet). Cost is reported as Rs 2,989 crore or Rs 2,389 crore, and the sources conflict. It is about 29 m taller than the 153 m Spring Temple Buddha.
claims.design_takeaway: Avoid any literal giant-statue gesture at ZMI. It would compete with, and look like a copy of, the Statue of Unity. A more architectural reference: the bronze-panel skin (thousands of small panels making one figure) as a metaphor for many parts making one whole, perhaps in a bronze-toned ceiling or facade made of thousands of panels.

sources.title: Guinness World Records: Tallest statue
sources.quote: Opened: Statue of Unity 'measures 182 m (597 ft 1 in) tall', 'located on a river island on the Narmada river', consecrated 31 October 2018.

sources.title: L&T Construction: Statue of Unity, Gujarat
sources.quote: Opened: 'The entire statue is clad with 6,500+ macro and micro bronze panels that sit on a concrete and steel superstructure' ... 'built in just 33 months to last a century'.

claims.claim: Ahmedabad is a key city of Indian modernism. Le Corbusier was invited after his first India visit in 1951 and designed four buildings there: the Mill Owners' Association building, the Museum (Sanskar Kendra), Villa Shodhan and Villa Sarabhai. Louis Kahn designed the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad campus from 1962, with B. V. Doshi as associate. Kahn's exposed brick was a material the client prescribed for economic reasons.
claims.detail: Le Corbusier (1953) on the Mill Owners' building: 'a little palace, genuine evidence of an architecture for modern times adjusted to the climate of India' (quoted in ArchDaily via Curtis). Kahn worked on IIM-A until his death in 1974; the campus is usually dated 1962-74. Exact Corbusier completion dates (about 1954-56) were not confirmed from sources opened here. Kahn's brick-and-arch dialogue ('I like an arch') comes from his talks to students, quoted in ArchDaily.
claims.design_takeaway: Use as background only. If ZMI's AMD zone needs a modern material voice next to sandstone jaali and carved timber, Kahn's load-bearing brick arches and circular cut-outs are recognisably Ahmedabad and suit Nagpur's climate. Keep it secondary to the vernacular references.

sources.title: ArchDaily: The Modernist Laboratory of the Future: Le Corbusier and Louis Kahn's Architecture in India
sources.quote: Opened: Mill Owners' building 'a little palace, genuine evidence of an architecture for modern times adjusted to the climate of India' (Le Corbusier, 1953); IIMA brick 'prescribed to him by the client due to economic restraints'.

sources.title: Pritzker Prize: Balkrishna Doshi
sources.quote: Opened: Doshi worked with Louis Kahn as an associate from 1962 'for over a decade' on IIM Ahmedabad.

claims.claim: Balkrishna Doshi (1927-2023), who worked under Le Corbusier and then Kahn, won the 2018 Pritzker Architecture Prize (announced 7 March 2018). He was the 45th laureate and 'the first to hail from India'. His Ahmedabad works include CEPT (founded as the School of Architecture, 1962-2012 in phases), Sangath (his studio, 1980) and Amdavad ni Gufa (1994).
claims.detail: Sangath means 'moving together' in Sanskrit (Pritzker jury material, search snippet). The Pritzker materials are promotional. Doshi also designed IIM Bangalore, which is in Bengaluru, not Ahmedabad; that is an interesting link to KIA/BLR for the merger story, but no source on it was opened here.
claims.design_takeaway: Doshi links Ahmedabad and Bengaluru: he lived in Ahmedabad and designed IIM Bangalore. That makes him a natural 'bridge' figure in ZMI's design narrative. Sangath's vaulted, half-sunken, water-channelled form also connects to the stepwell idea.

sources.title: Pritzker Prize: Balkrishna Doshi
sources.quote: Opened: 2018 laureate, 'the first to hail from India'; works listed include Sangath (1980), Amdavad Ni Gufa (1994), CEPT (1966-2012); 'I owe this prestigious prize to my guru, Le Corbusier.'

claims.claim: On 12 June 2025, Air India flight AI171, a Boeing 787-8 from Ahmedabad to London Gatwick, crashed shortly after take-off from SVPIA into the BJ Medical College hostel area just under a nautical mile from the runway. 241 of the 242 people on board died, and about 19 people were killed on the ground.
claims.detail: The AAIB preliminary report (12 July 2025) found both engines' fuel-control switches moved to CUTOFF within about one second, and did not assign a cause. As of December 2025 the investigation was ongoing (Khaleej Times). Whether a final report has been published was not checked. Total deaths reported as about 260 including ground casualties.
claims.design_takeaway: AMD is now associated in public memory with a recent mass-casualty accident. The game should not script crash scenarios themed on Ahmedabad or AI171, and the design document's Ahmedabad section should stay respectful. A quiet memorial space in the AMD-derived zone may be appropriate, but it needs care and should not be used as gameplay.

sources.title: Al Jazeera, 12 Jul 2025: How Air India flight 171 crashed and its fatal last moments
sources.quote: Opened: departed 'At 13:38 [08:08 GMT] on the afternoon of June 12' for London Gatwick with '230 passengers, 10 cabin crew and 2 pilots'; 'All but one of the people on board the plane were killed'; 'Some 19 people on the ground were also killed'.

open_questions: Who designed SVPIA T1 and the 2010 T2? No architect or consultant could be found in AAI records, trade press or news. An AAI RTI request or 2008-2010 tender documents would settle it.

Has Adani appointed an architect or published a design concept for the New Integrated Terminal Building (construction started by July 2026)? If a heritage-themed design appears later, ZMI's AMD references should be checked against it so they do not look derivative.
Is there a measured temperature difference for Adalaj or any Gujarat stepwell? The widely quoted 5-6 °C appears unmeasured. The Cardiff University Jodhpur stepwell study (ICUC12) may publish numbers.

Adalaj entrance orientation conflicts: the Athens Journal (2021) says the three stairs come from south, west and east with the long axis north-south; Studio Matrx says north, south and east. A plan drawing (Jain-Neubauer, 'The Stepwells of Gujarat', 1981) would resolve it before ZMI copies the plan.

Number of pols in the walled city: sources give about 360, about 600 and 6,000. The ICOMOS 2017 evaluation (whc.unesco.org/document/159757) probably has the authoritative figure, but UNESCO pages returned 403 to every fetch.

Were the 'Aangan Van' planters (Dholavira-script motifs) actually built in T2 after the August 2023 announcement, and does the 350 m 'Conversations of Freedom' mural (Sept 2025) exist as described? It rests on one travel-site article.

Was the Statue of Unity also sculpted by Ram Sutar, who made the 18 ft Patel statue at SVPIA? That would give the airport statue and the national monument the same author, which is good for the narrative, but no source was opened to confirm it.
Is a memorial for AI171 (12 June 2025) planned at or near SVPIA? This affects how respectfully ZMI should treat the closing of AMD.

verdicts.corrected_claim: SVPIA's current international terminal (today's T2) was inaugurated in early July 2010 by Praful Patel, then Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Civil Aviation. A narendramodi.in report dated 4 July 2010 (seen only as a search snippet) gives the cost as Rs 290 crore. Wikipedia gives 5 July. Another reported cost figure is Rs 316 crore (Deccan Herald, search snippet). The terminal opened to the public in September 2010. Airport-technology.com profiles the 2010 building, which it labels the 'new Terminal 3', as 41,000 m2 with 4 aerobridges and 32 check-in counters. It says the building was built in two phases, first by Italian-Thai Development with Pratibha Consortium and then by M S Khurana Engineering, and was 'designed based on the Singapore Changi Airport' following IATA guidelines. No architect is named anywhere. The 7,825 m2 / 23-counter figure on that page belongs to the older international terminal, not the 2010 building.
verdicts.note: I opened airport-technology.com. It lists three buildings: T1 (domestic, 30 counters), T2 (international, 7,825 m2, 23 counters), and a 'new Terminal 3' opened to the public in September 2010 at 41,000 m2. The researcher wrongly applied the 7,825 m2 figure to today's T2. The 41,000 m2 figure for the 2010 building fits today's 49,000 m2 T2 plus the 2,550 m2 (2023) and 2,100 m2 (2024) extensions. The 'Changi' design claim is therefore not Wikipedia-only; a trade profile states it. Contractors are named, but no architect is. narendramodi.in timed out on both WebFetch and curl, and eparlib (the Lok Sabha source) would not resolve. The search summary gives the narendramodi.in date as 4 July 2010 and also cites Deccan Herald at Rs 316 crore; Deccan Herald returned 403 when fetched. The DeshGujarat 2011 article confirms that Praful Patel opened 'a newly constructed international terminal' the previous year. The design takeaway (that SVPIA's building form is not DNA-worthy) still holds.

sources.quote: Opened: 'The terminal was opened for public in September 2010' ... 'covers an area of 41,000m²' ... 'four aerobridges and 32 check-in counters' ... 'designed based on the Singapore Changi Airport' ... first phase by 'Italian Thai Development (ITD) and Mumbai-based Pratibha Consortium', second by 'M S Khurana Engineering Limited'.

The Adani media note of 13 May 2025 confirms the 'extended check-in hall' and the 'inter-terminal electric shuttle buses' (I extracted the PDF text locally). One small oddity: the Aug 2023 arrivals block had 24 immigration counters, while the 2026 article says 22 arrival counters plus e-gates.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Adani Ahmedabad International Airport Ltd took over SVPIA from the Airports Authority of India at midnight on 6/7 November 2020. It holds a 50-year lease covering operations, management and development. AAI keeps customs, immigration, plant and animal quarantine, and security. Business Today reports that commercial operations began on Sunday 8 November 2020.
verdicts.note: I opened The Week (7 Nov 2020), which says the handover took effect 'from midnight on Friday' (6 Nov), covers 50 years, and leaves 'customs, immigration, plant and animal quarantine and security' with AAI. Business Today (8 Nov 2020) says the handover was on 6 November and the takeover and commercial operations on Sunday, so it is internally loose but consistent with a 6/7 Nov midnight handover. The search summary says the concession agreement was signed on 14 Feb 2020 and that AAI extended the takeover deadline to 12 Nov 2020 because of COVID; that came from search snippets only.

verdicts.corrected_claim: SVPIA handled 13,427,697 passengers in FY2024-25 (1 Apr 2024 to 31 Mar 2025), up 14.8% from 11,696,227. That was over 11 million domestic and over 2.2 million international passengers, with 101,119 aircraft movements (up 16.2% from 87,025). Its record day was 25 January 2025: 48,137 passengers and 351 movements.
verdicts.note: I extracted the text of the operator PDF locally with pdftotext, and every figure matches exactly. The same note gives the previous record as 42,224 passengers and 328 movements on 20 Nov 2023, and about 36,800 passengers and 288 flights per day to 48 domestic and 16 international destinations. DeshGujarat (Aug 2025) uses '1.2 crore in FY 2025', which conflicts with this; the operator figure should win.

verdicts.corrected_claim: In August 2023 the operator opened a 2,550 m2 international arrival block in T2 with 24 immigration counters (up from 16) and six baggage belts. Its stated design theme is 'Amaru Amdavad' (My Amdavad), and the release explicitly cites Ahmedabad being 'the first world heritage city'. It describes passengers passing 'beneath an array of shimmering torans' and promises 'Aangan Van' planters showing regional culture 'through Dholavira encryption', to form 'a sky-lit indoor oasis'. The wording leaves unclear whether the torans and planters were installed or still planned.
verdicts.note: I extracted the full text of the Adani PDF of 24 Aug 2023 locally, and every quoted phrase is present. The planters are described as part of 'ongoing art projects' with art and craft 'will be added soon'. Even the toran sentence ends with 'in the near future', so whether either was installed is unconfirmed.

'"Aangan Van" planters ... through Dholavira encryption' ... 'six impressive spacious baggage belts'.

verdicts.corrected_claim: SVPIA expresses local identity mainly through art installations. In January 2022 it had 'Wave of Life', a fabric kite installation by Idea Factor about 150 m long across the airport facade, welcoming the New Year 2022 and linked to the kite festival. It also had carved Gujarati wooden panels at T2, a haveli-style carved wooden arch near the T1 baggage belts, and Kutch embroidered textiles in T1 departures. In September 2025, T2 unveiled a series of artworks (News Arena, 16 Sep 2025). Per a single travel-site source, these include a 350 m metallic mural with jaali-style illustrations ('Conversations of Freedom', on Gandhi and Sardar Patel), an 'Utsav Wall' for Navratri and Uttarayan, and 'Pragati-ni-Patang', bronze children with illuminated acrylic kites.
verdicts.note: I opened the AviationPros release of 12 Jan 2022. It says 'Wave of Life' was 'welcoming the New year 2022' and ties it to the kite festival, but it does not use the phrase 'kite season'. It also lists 'Patterns of Gujarat' (fabric discs by CEPT-trained designer Tarang Sagra) and six Vaishnav Dwarpal figures in T1 arrivals. I opened IndianEagle (17 Sep 2025), which confirms the 350 m, jaali, Gandhi/Patel, Utsav Wall and Pragati-ni-Patang details. News Arena confirms only that a series of T2 installations was unveiled on 16 Sep 2025, with no specifics. The 350 m figure remains single-sourced.

verdicts.corrected_claim: An 18 ft statue of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel by sculptor Ram Sutar was unveiled at SVPIA on 9 January 2011 by Civil Aviation Minister Praful Patel. AAI paid Rs 50 lakh for it, and it was described as possibly the tallest statue of Patel in Gujarat at the time.
verdicts.note: DeshGujarat gives the height, sculptor and cost. Its headline is dated 8 Jan and is in future tense ('to dedicate'). A PIB photo caption I opened independently confirms the unveiling took place on 9 January 2011 with Praful Patel and Dinsha Patel present. The search tool said the airport statue was the model for the Statue of Unity, but that came from a Wikipedia-derived snippet and is unverified.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Adani is building a New Integrated Terminal Building (NITB) at SVPIA that will combine domestic and international operations. Swarajya (29 Jul 2026, citing the Times of India) reports that construction has begun, that phase 1 is 'estimated to cost more than Rs 3,000 crore' and is targeted for 2029-30, and that the building sits 'adjacent to the existing domestic terminal, extending from the T3 side' ('T3 has nearly been vacated'). An earlier DeshGujarat report (7 Aug 2025) gave an 'estimated project cost exceeding ₹3,100 crore' without saying which phase it covers. It also reported two phases to be finished before 2036, over 10 aerobridges, capacity rising to 2 crore passengers a year, and T1 to be demolished. No architect or design concept is named in either source.
verdicts.note: I opened both articles. The claim treats Rs 3,000-3,100 crore as the phase 1 cost, but only Swarajya ties its figure (more than Rs 3,000 crore) to phase 1. DeshGujarat attaches Rs 3,100 crore to 'the new integrated terminal' generally, so the figures should be kept separate. The other details match: construction 'has commenced', the T3 side, and 2029-30. DeshGujarat's '1.2 crore in FY 2025' baseline conflicts with the operator's 1.34 crore. The Benoy FBO page returned only site navigation, so the Benoy concepts remain unverifiable. I could not search to confirm that no rendering has been published.

verdicts.corrected_claim: The 'Historic City of Ahmadabad' is the walled city founded in the 15th century (1411, per UNESCO) by Sultan Ahmad Shah on the eastern bank of the Sabarmati. It was inscribed on the World Heritage List on 8 July 2017 at the 41st session of the World Heritage Committee in Kraków, under criteria (ii) and (v). The Government of India describes it as the first Indian city, and the third in Asia, to be inscribed. The property includes 28 ASI centrally protected monuments.
verdicts.note: PIB returned 403 to WebFetch, so I fetched it with curl. The release (Ministry of Culture, 10 Jul 2017) confirms the date of 8 July 2017, the 41st session, criteria (ii) and (v), 'first city in India and the third in Asia', 'eastern bank of the Sabarmati', '28 ASI Centrally Protected Monuments', and that the proposal 'had earlier been deferred'. The official 41COM decisions PDF, which I downloaded from whc.unesco.org, confirms the inscription on criteria (ii) and (v) at 'Krakow, 2017' and names Sultan Ahmed Shah. The year 1411, the 535.7 ha area and the 2,696 AMC-protected buildings all come from UNESCO list pages that return 403, so I could not verify them.

verdicts.corrected_claim: UNESCO's 2017 inscription decision describes the walled city's settlement fabric as pur (neighbourhoods), pol (residential main streets) and khadki (inner entrances to the pol). The AMC Heritage Department page, fetched with curl, confirms the cell was set up in July 1996 with CRUTA Foundation as 'the first heritage cell in India within an Urban Local Body', that the heritage walk was 'launched in 1997', and that it has restored 'more than 20 old Chabutras'. verdicts.corrected_claim: The Sidi Saiyyed mosque, completed around 1572/73 CE (AMC says 1573) just before the Mughal conquest of Gujarat, is the last major Gujarat Sultanate monument. Its sandstone window screens (jalis) include a 'tree-of-life'-and-parasite window: a single palm with spreading fronds, wrapped by a flowering vine that emerges from the mouth of a makara. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation says the jalis 'have become a symbol of the city of Ahmedabad'.
verdicts.note: I extracted the full IIMA PDF text and opened the AMC page. IIMA confirms: 'completed around 1572/73 CE, just before Akbar conquered Gujarat'; 'last major example of the Gujarat Sultanate style'; ten windows (three north, three south, four west, two on either side of a blind middle space); the palm, the vine and the makara; the rati-kera creeper pattern; Sidi Saiyad as a Habshi who died on 24 Dec 1576. AMC confirms 'completed in 1573', 'hewn from solid stone', that the central arch 'is actually walled with stone', the unfinished state 'before the Mughals invaded Gujarat', and the 'symbol of the city' wording. IIMA adds that Sidi Saiyad converted an older brick mosque into the present structure, possibly between 1570 and 1573.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Adalaj stepwell (Rudabai ni Vav) lies about 13-19 km north of Ahmedabad (the Athens Journal says about 13 km; Gujarat Tourism says 19 km). Its date is 1498 or 1499 CE: Studio Matrx gives 1498 'inscribed', Incredible India says 'construction began in 1498', and the Athens Journal gives 1499. Its 27-line Sanskrit inscription praises Queen Rudabai (Rudadevi), wife or widow of the Vaghela chief Rana Veer Singh. The claim that Sultan Mahmud Begada completed it belongs to the popular narrative repeated by Incredible India and the Athens paper; I could not confirm it from the inscription. It is a five-storey trabeate sandstone structure about 75 m long (the Athens Journal gives 75.3 m, oriented north-south). Its three entrance stairs meet at the first underground storey on a large square platform with an octagonal opening above, carried on 16 pillars. From there a stepped descent leads to the well.
verdicts.note: I extracted the Athens Journal paper locally. It describes 'a huge square platform. This platform has an octagonal opening', so the landing is square, not octagonal. It gives about 13 km north of Ahmedabad, 75.3 m long (also '250 feet'), south entrance with stairs to the south, west and east, a 'Jaya' type (three entrances), and a 27-line Sanskrit inscription on a marble slab. The paper is internally inconsistent: it says 'late 16th century' and 'By 1599 A.D.' in places, and mentions 'arched openings' despite calling the structure trabeated. Treat it as weak. I did not find the Samvat 1555 date in any page I opened. Studio Matrx gives 1498 CE 'inscribed; high confidence' and places the entrances north, south and east, so the orientation conflict stands. Incredible India gives the Veer Singh / Begada / Rudabai legend as history. Gujarat Tourism's 'built by Mahmud Begada in 1411' and '19km north' are confirmed as what that page says.

'The three entrances meet in the first storey below-ground in a huge square platform. This platform has an octagonal opening and rests on 16 pillars'.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Adalaj is widely described as about 5-6 °C cooler at its lower levels than at ground level. The 2021 Athens Journal of Architecture paper itself states a '5 to 6 degrees temperature drop', but like the other sources it gives no measurement, instrument or date. So the figure is repeated widely but has never been shown to be measured. The paper attributes the cooling to the thermal mass of stone and ground and to evaporation from the shaded water.
verdicts.note: The researcher said the Athens paper describes the cooling only qualitatively. That is wrong: I extracted the PDF, and later in the text it says the stepwell 'will always have a 5 to 6 degrees temperature drop compared to the outside ambient temperature', attributed to 'slow evaporation rates of the water which is shaded on all sides by massive walls'. No measurement backs it. The paper is also internally inconsistent on dates, so it is a weak source; I would not call it peer-reviewed evidence. Gujarat Tourism hedges with 'It is said ... six degrees cooler'. Studio Matrx says 'five to six degrees Celsius', uncited. Incredible India is qualitative only. The ICUC12 abstract (Sharmin et al., Cardiff) on Jodhpur stepwells describes measurements of air temperature, relative humidity, globe temperature and wind with 300 survey respondents, but reports no figures yet.

sources.quote: Opened: microclimate measurements (air temperature, RH, globe temperature, wind speed) and a 300-person thermal comfort survey at a Jodhpur stepwell; no numeric temperature differences reported.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen's Stepwell) at Patan, Gujarat, was built in the 11th century CE, traditionally dated 1063, by Queen Udayamati of the Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty as a memorial to King Bhimdev I. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014 (38th session, Doha, criteria (i) and (iv)). UNESCO describes it as 'an inverted temple highlighting the sanctity of water', divided into seven levels of stairs, with more than 500 principal and over 1,000 minor sculptures.
verdicts.note: I downloaded the official 38COM decisions PDF (Doha, 2014) from whc.unesco.org. Decision 38 COM 8B.25 confirms criteria (i) and (iv), 'Initially built as a memorial in the 11th century CE', 'inverted temple highlighting the sanctity of water', 'seven levels of stairs', and 'More than five hundred principle sculptures and over a thousand minor ones'. The UNESCO text does not name the queen. Gujarat Tourism gives '1063', 'Rani Udayamati of the Chaulukya Dynasty' and Bhimdev I. Gujarat Tourism also says the ASI 'restored it in 1980s' and 'more than 800 sculptures'. The ASI page loaded only site chrome, so the tank and shaft dimensions remain unverified.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Ahmedabad is a key city of Indian modernism. Le Corbusier was invited after his first India visit in 1951 and designed four buildings there: the Mill Owners' Association building, the Museum (Sanskar Kendra), Villa Shodhan and Villa Sarabhai. Louis Kahn designed the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad campus from 1962, with B. V. Doshi as associate. Kahn's exposed brick was a material the client prescribed for economic reasons.
verdicts.note: I opened the ArchDaily article. It gives four buildings (a museum, the Millowners' Association Building, the Shodhan dwellings, and a house for Manorama Sarabhai), the 1951 first visit followed by an Ahmedabad invitation, the 1953 'little palace' quote, and brick 'prescribed to him by the client' for economic reasons. Doshi says Kahn accepted on condition that Doshi join as associate. The Pritzker page gives 1962 as the start of Doshi's associate work with Kahn. ArchDaily does not use the name 'Sanskar Kendra'.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Balkrishna Doshi (1927-2023) worked under Le Corbusier, returning to India in 1954 to oversee Le Corbusier's Chandigarh and Ahmedabad projects, and then worked with Kahn. He won the 2018 Pritzker Architecture Prize (announced 7 March 2018) as its 45th laureate and 'the first to hail from India'. The Pritzker list of his works includes CEPT, Ahmedabad (1966-2012), Sangath, Ahmedabad (1980), Amdavad ni Gufa (1994) and IIM Bangalore (1977-1992).

The researcher said the IIM Bangalore link was unverified, but the same Pritzker page lists 'Indian Institute of Management Bangalore (1977–1992)', so the Doshi link between Ahmedabad and Bengaluru is now sourced. The meaning of 'Sangath' ('moving together') was not verified.

claims.claim: Nagpur's Zero Mile monument has two sandstone elements. One is a pillar. The other is a small stone marking a Great Trigonometrical Survey (GTS) Standard Bench Mark, inscribed "G.T.S. STANDARD BENCH MARK. 1907". An inscription records the pillar top as 1,020.171 ft (310.948 m) above mean sea level. The site is south-east of the Vidhan Bhavan (state legislature building) in central Nagpur.
claims.detail: Coordinates: about 21°08'59"N 79°04'50"E (Wikipedia). Wikipedia says distances are cut into the hexagonal base in miles: Raipur 174 mi (E), Hyderabad 318 mi, Chandrapur 125 mi, Jabalpur 170 mi, Seoni 79 mi, Chhindwara 83 mi, Betul 101 mi (W). Only Wikipedia gives that table. The Better India and Incredible India say only that distances are engraved. Incredible India calls it a sandstone pillar that 'served as a crucial point for measuring distances between major towns and cities'.
claims.design_takeaway: The physical vocabulary to borrow is a stone datum pillar, a benchmark height and distances in miles cut into a hexagonal base. A ZMI forecourt or central hall could hold a datum pillar giving distances to AMD, BOM and BLR and the elevation of the terminal floor. The airport sits at 306-320 m AMSL, very close to the stone's 311 m.
