claims.claim: Four stucco horses stand beside the pillar, and sources say they were added well after 1907. The monument is neglected and under restoration. In January 2023 CREDAI Nagpur's plan covering 'the four horses, sand stone, and the Zero Mile pillar' was approved. In March 2025 the Heritage Conservation Committee told Nagpur Municipal Corporation to seek custody from the District Collectorate, with PWD doing the restoration and Indian Oil CSR funds requested.
claims.detail: In 2023 two of the four horses had cracks. Wikipedia and Hitavada 2025 call the horses 'stucco' and 'added later'. No source found gives the year the horses were added or who added them. Wikipedia cites a 2008 Times of India pledge to maintain the monument for 5 years. I did not open the original TOI piece.
claims.design_takeaway: The four horses facing outward are the part people recognise. Four directional figures around a central datum fit a hub whose job is to send flows out in all directions. The ZMI concept is literally three cities merging into one centre, so a four-way motif can carry 'three origins plus the new hub'.

sources.title: Zero Mile's prime glory to be restored (The Hitavada, 2023)
sources.quote: Opened. Plan covers "the four horses, sand stone, and the Zero Mile pillar"; of the four horses "two had developed cracks".

sources.title: Seek custody of Zero Mile: HCC directs NMC (The Hitavada, 7 Mar 2025)
sources.quote: Opened. Four stucco horses beside the stone, added much later; District Collectorate oversees it; HCC asks NMC to seek custody; CM asked IOC to fund restoration via CSR; PWD entrusted with renovation.

claims.claim: The usual account is that the British erected the monument during the Raj in connection with the Great Trigonometrical Survey, and the benchmark stone is dated 1907. No source I found names a specific agency, officer or date for the pillar itself, as distinct from the benchmark.
claims.detail: '1907' is the date inscribed on the benchmark stone. Sources turn it into 'built in 1907' (Wikipedia) or 'erected in 1907, when the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India began' (Hitavada 2025). The Hitavada wording is historically wrong. From background knowledge, not a source opened here: the GTS began in 1802 under William Lambton, and its main triangulation was largely done by the 1870s. A 1907 date fits the later levelling and benchmark network better than the GTS founding. One search snippet, from an aaroads wiki page that returned 403 when I tried to open it, said there is 'no verifiable evidence' that the British erected the stone as the point from which to measure all distances. Incredible India links it to the GTS but gives no date or builder.
claims.design_takeaway: In ZMI materials, say 'a GTS benchmark dated 1907', not 'built by the GTS in 1907 to mark the centre'. The honest reading, a survey datum and not a proven centroid, makes a stronger concept anyway: ZMI as the new datum of Indian aviation.

sources.title: The Better India
sources.quote: Opened. Monument "was constructed during the time of the Raj"; G.T.S refers to the Great Trigonometrical Survey, a 19th-century Survey of India project.

sources.title: The Hitavada, 7 Mar 2025
sources.quote: Opened. States the stone was erected in 1907, when the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India began (this framing is chronologically wrong; see detail).

sources.title: Incredible India - Zero Mile Marker
sources.quote: Opened. "the Zero Mile Marker played a central role in their Great Trigonometrical Survey of India" (no builder or date given).

claims.claim: It is widely said that the Zero Mile stone marks the geographic centre of (colonial) India, but this is contested and not officially verified. The Government of India's tourism site calls the claim 'debatable'. Two Madhya Pradesh villages, Karaundi (Jabalpur district) and Barsali (Betul district), are put forward as the centre of post-1947 India.
claims.detail: Hitavada (2025) also says the stone shows the directions of nine metros (Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Kochi, Mumbai, Kolkata, New Delhi, Pune) and that 'all nine cities are equidistant' from it. That is false: by road Mumbai is about 800 km away, Delhi about 1,000 km and Kochi more than 1,300 km. Treat it as civic folklore. Britannica (search snippet only; the page returned 403) says Nagpur is 'situated almost at the geographic centre of the country'. MIHAN India Ltd's site uses the tagline 'Connecting miles through zero mile'.
claims.design_takeaway: Frame the site as 'India's zero mile', a symbolic datum. Do not call it the 'exact geographic centre' in citations. Nagpur's centrality between the four big metros is real and defensible as an airline-network argument even if the centroid claim is not.

sources.title: Incredible India - Zero Mile Marker
sources.quote: Opened. "although its claim as the exact geographic centre of India remains debatable."

sources.title: The Better India
sources.quote: Opened. Centre reportedly shifted after partition: "It is now supposed to be in Karaundi, located about 40 km from Sihora in Jabalpur district."

sources.title: The Hitavada, 7 Mar 2025
sources.quote: Opened. Lists nine metros and says they are equidistant from the stone (factually doubtful).

sources.title: MIHAN India Limited (airport operator JV)
sources.quote: Opened. Tagline "Connecting miles through zero mile"; Nagpur's 'Zero Mile Center' nickname comes from its location at India's geographic center.

claims.claim: Nagpur's highest temperature on record, according to IMD Nagpur's May climatic-features sheet, is 47.9 °C on 23 May 2013. The previous high was 47.8 °C on 26 May 1954.
claims.detail: I saw the IMD sheet only as a search snippet. The PDF itself (imdnagpur.gov.in) refused connections. Al Jazeera (23 May 2013, opened) confirms 'Nagpur saw the mercury rise to 47.9C'. A 2020 Hindustan Times piece (snippet; PressReader returned 403) gives 47.9 °C on 23 May 2013 as the all-time high, with 47.8 °C (1954), 47.7 °C (2003), 47.6 °C (2005) and 47.5 °C (28 May 2019). A weather blog dates the reading to 22 May and says it was logged under 23 May. Conflicting figures: the Nagpur district website (opened) says '48.6 degrees Celsius' on 29 May 2012, and a blog cites 48.6 °C on 24 May 1954 at an old observatory. Neither matches IMD, so treat both as unreliable. Recent peaks have been lower, for example the 2024 season high of 45.6 °C on 27 May (Hitavada).
claims.design_takeaway: Design the envelope, apron surfaces, cooling plant and passenger heat-safety systems for a 48 °C design extreme with margin. The game's heat events can cite '47.9 °C, 23 May 2013' as the real record.

sources.title: IMD RMC Nagpur - Climatic features of Nagpur, May
sources.quote: Search snippet only (server unreachable): highest maximum 47.9 °C on 23 May 2013; mean maximum 43.1 °C.

sources.title: India heats up (Al Jazeera, 23 May 2013)
sources.quote: Opened. "Nagpur saw the mercury rise to 47.9C"

sources.title: Geography & climate - Nagpur district (Govt of Maharashtra)
sources.quote: Opened. "On May 29, 2012, the city recorded 48.6 degrees Celsius." (conflicts with IMD)

sources.title: Hindustan Times (24 May 2020) via PressReader
sources.quote: Search snippet only: "the all-time high was recorded on 47.9 degrees Celsius on May 23, 2013"; 47.5 °C on May 28 (2019).

claims.claim: May is Nagpur's hottest month: IMD gives a mean maximum of 43.1 °C and a mean minimum of 27.8 °C, and the year's peak usually comes in the last week of May. Nagpur has more heat-wave days than any other city in Maharashtra: 107 May heat-wave days and 246 in total over 1969-2019.
claims.detail: The IMD figures come from a search snippet of the RMC Nagpur May sheet. The heat-wave counts are from The Hitavada (11 May 2022, opened), which cites IMD data. IMD thresholds quoted there: heat wave when absolute Tmax ≥45 °C, severe ≥47 °C, or a departure of 4.5-6.4 °C above normal. Incredible India's monthly chart (opened) shows May maxima around 46 °C.
claims.design_takeaway: Long, sun-exposed landside walks and kerbs are a real hazard from April to June. Use shaded or enclosed forecourts, shaded rail and metro interchanges, and night-weighted operations. In the game, May can be a high-heat season with crew and ramp-worker constraints.

sources.title: IMD RMC Nagpur - Climatic features of Nagpur, May
sources.quote: Search snippet only: "The mean maximum temperature is 43.1°C during the month"; highest temperature typically in last week of May; mean minimum 27.8 °C.

sources.title: Nagpur records highest heat wave days in May in last 50 years (The Hitavada, 2022)
sources.quote: Opened. "Nagpur city experienced the highest 107 days of heat waves during the month of May in last 50 years"; 246 annual heat-wave days.

claims.claim: Nagpur's average annual rainfall is about 1,050-1,100 mm, and nearly all of it falls in the south-west monsoon from June to September. The normal onset is now about 15 June. It used to be 10 June.
claims.detail: The district website (opened) gives 'average annual rainfall of 1064.1 mm' and, in the same place, '1205 mm' for June-September, which is inconsistent. Its climate table gives 1,094 mm (NOAA 1971-1990). Hitavada (29 Sep 2021, opened) quotes IMD scientist M L Sahu: onset 'Earlier... June 10 but the new date is June 15'. The city has had more than 1,000 mm every year since 2015, and 2021 reached 1,246.3 mm by late September. Withdrawal is around early October. IMD's Maharashtra climate statement (snippet) says the SW monsoon brings about 88.4% of the state's annual rain (1971-2020). I did not find an official IMD 1991-2020 normal for Nagpur station.
claims.design_takeaway: Use about 1,100 mm a year, concentrated in roughly 100 days, for roof drainage, rainwater harvesting and the stormwater design of a very large roof. The monsoon (June-September) is a distinct operating season for the game: thunderstorm holds, waterlogged landside, low-visibility approaches.

sources.title: Geography & climate - Nagpur district
sources.quote: Opened. "Nagpur district has an average annual rainfall of 1064.1 mm." "During the monsoon of June to September, Nagpur has 1205 mm of rain."

sources.title: City witnesses trend of increasing annual rainfall in last one decade (The Hitavada, 2021)
sources.quote: Opened. "Earlier, the onset was June 10 but the new date is June 15." Over 1,000 mm every year since 2015.

sources.title: IMD Statement on Climate for Maharashtra 2022
sources.quote: Search snippet only: SW monsoon season contributes about 88.4% of Maharashtra's annual rainfall (1971-2020 climatology).

claims.claim: Before the monsoon, in April and May, Vidarbha including Nagpur gets afternoon and evening thunderstorms, sometimes with hail and gusts of 40-50 km/h. IMD issues orange alerts for these, for example on 9-10 April 2024, 3-4 April 2025 and 7-9 May 2024.
claims.detail: I found no source quantifying dust-storm frequency at Nagpur. IMD's FAQ defines dust storms, but nothing I found gives Nagpur-specific numbers. IMD's April climatic sheet (snippet) says squalls and hail are only occasional. Treat 'dust season' as unverified. Thunderstorm, squall and hail risk from March to May is well documented.
claims.design_takeaway: Plan for convective weather in the hottest months: wind uplift on large roof spans, hail on glazing and skylights, and lightning holds on ramp work. In the game, April-May can bring short thunderstorm and hail 'ramp closure' events between heat waves.

sources.title: Heavy rains lash city, IMD issues 'Orange Alert' for Apr 10 (The Hitavada, 2024)
sources.quote: Search snippet only: orange alert for Vidarbha; hailstorms, thunderstorms and gusty winds of 40-50 kmph likely.

sources.title: Gusty winds, showers, hail storm - a very unlikely picture in May (The Hitavada, 2024)
sources.quote: Search snippet only: hail in parts of Nagpur; IMD forecast thunderstorm, gusty winds 40-50 kmph and hail 7-9 May.

claims.claim: Nagpur district sits mainly on Deccan Trap basalt, with Gondwana, Lameta and Archean rocks and alluvium also present, and its soils are black soils of varying depth. An ICAR-CRIDA district plan using NBSS&LUP data classes about 43% of the district as deep black soil, 14% as medium-deep and 43% as shallow. These clay-rich black 'regur' soils swell when wet and shrink and crack when dry.
claims.detail: The ICAR-CRIDA percentages (deep black 427.9 thousand ha, 43.4%; medium deep 136.4, 13.8%; shallow 421.5, 42.7%) come from a search snippet. The PDF itself was unreachable. CGWB's Nagpur aquifer report (opened by download) records 'Black cotton soil' at one infiltration-test site and 'clayey moderately deep' and 'moderately deep loamy' soils at others. So conditions vary, and site-specific geotechnical investigation is essential. Standard Indian practice on expansive soils: found below the seasonal active zone using under-reamed piles (IS 2911 Part 3), rafts or a cohesive non-swelling (CNS) replacement layer. That comes from general engineering sources and a 1978 IGS lecture, not a Nagpur-specific study.
claims.design_takeaway: For a 4+ km runway system and very long terminal piers, assume expansive black-cotton soil at the top and basalt below. Budget for deep or under-reamed piling, moisture-controlled subgrades and CNS layers under pavements. 'Black earth' is also a strong regional material and colour reference for landscape and plinths.

sources.title: ICAR-CRIDA District Agriculture Contingency Plan - Nagpur
sources.quote: Search snippet only (server unreachable): "Deep black soils 427.9 (43.4%); medium deep black soils 136.4 (13.8%); shallow black soils 421.5 (42.7%)".

sources.title: CGWB - Aquifer mapping report, Nagpur district
sources.quote: Opened (text extracted). Soil infiltration test annex lists 'Soil Type: Black cotton soil' at one site; geology lists Alluvium, Deccan Trap Basalt, Lameta, Gondwana, Archean.

sources.title: Indian Geotechnical Society annual lecture 1978 (black cotton soil behaviour)
sources.quote: Search snippet only: damage to canal linings, bed heaving and buildings in black cotton soil; CNS layer used as mitigation (Karnataka case, not Nagpur).

claims.claim: Nagpur is known as the 'Orange City' because of the Nagpur mandarin (Citrus reticulata Blanco), which received a Geographical Indication tag in 2014. Nagpur district alone had 21,973.6 ha of mandarin orchards producing 131,841.6 t in 2021-22.
claims.detail: The district figures come from a Plant Archives paper (opened by download) citing Indiastat. Wider figures disagree. A DailyO piece (snippet, about 2017) gives Maharashtra about 1.21 lakh ha (121,000 ha) of oranges, with Amravati district at 56,747 ha. A Sentinel editorial (snippet) gives about 80,000 ha across Vidarbha. Vidarbha has two crops a year, Ambia and Mrig (snippet, blog source). Down to Earth (Oct 2024) reports that heat waves cause fruit drop. I found no current official Vidarbha-wide orchard area.
claims.design_takeaway: Orange is the obvious regional colour and material cue, for wayfinding accents and orchard landscaping on the landside approaches. Orchard grids around the site could form a heat-buffering green belt. The two harvests and perishable fruit justify a cold-chain cargo node in the game and the masterplan.

sources.title: Nagpur - Incredible India
sources.quote: Opened. Nagpur is "Nicknamed the 'Orange City'"; orange orchards outside the city.

sources.title: GI tag for Nagpur orange to benefit both farmers and consumers (Down To Earth, 1 Sep 2014)
sources.quote: Opened. Fruit is Citrus reticulata Blanco (Nagpur mandarin), recently given GI tag; grower registration about Rs 1,500 for 10 years.

sources.title: Economic feasibility and constraints analysis of mandarin orange cultivation in Nagpur district (Plant Archives)
sources.quote: Opened. "Nagpur district alone accounted for 21,973.6 hectares area with production of 131841.6 metric tons of mandarin orange production in the year (2021-22)".

sources.title: DTE ground report: climate change threatens Nagpur oranges (Down To Earth, 12 Oct 2024)
sources.quote: Opened. Nagpur is known as the "Orange City"; heat waves cause premature fruit drop.

claims.claim: Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar International Airport (NAG/VANP) is at Sonegaon, 8 km south-west of Nagpur, at 306-320 m AMSL. It has one 3,200 m runway, 14/32, about 45-46 m wide. NH44 runs 0.31 km from the site, Khapri railway station is 4.9 km south and Ajni 5 km north-east.
claims.detail: From MIHAN India Ltd's pre-feasibility report filed for environmental clearance (Nov 2021, opened by download). That report says the current 3,200 m runway and its sub-base restrict regular Code E wide-body operations. Width is 46 m per SKYbrary (snippet). Traffic: about 2.9 million passengers in FY2024-25 (Wikipedia snippet), and about 2.69 million in January-November 2025 (Navbharat snippet). Stated capacity is about 3-3.5 million passengers a year. The Nag River stream runs next to the site.
claims.design_takeaway: NAG is a small (about 3 Mppa) single-runway airport hemmed in by the city and NH44. A ZMI-scale hub (combined DEL+BOM+BLR+HYD traffic, well over 200 Mppa) cannot grow out of it. That supports a greenfield site south of the city along the NH44 / Samruddhi / rail corridor, and makes NAG a likely candidate to close or be repurposed.

sources.title: PFR for the Expansion of Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar International Airport, Nagpur (MIHAN India Ltd, Nov 2021)
sources.quote: Opened. "The airport is located at Sonegaon, 8 km South-West of Nagpur... altitude of 306-320 m above MSL"; "the present runway only has a length of 3200 m"; "Nearest Highway NH-44... 0.31 km"; "Khapri R.S. - 4.9 km, S".

sources.title: SKYbrary - VANP
sources.quote: Search snippet only: runway 14/32, 3200 m, width 46 m.

claims.claim: GMR Nagpur International Airport Ltd (GNIAL) took over NAG from MIHAN India Ltd on 25 June 2026 under a 30-year concession. GMR's plan, announced 8-9 July 2026, raises capacity from about 3 Mppa to 30 Mppa, with potential for 50 Mppa. It runs in three phases: about Rs 300 crore of upgrades over 12-18 months; a new integrated terminal (initial 4 Mppa) and a 20,000 t/yr cargo terminal in years 3-4; and a second runway, new ATC tower and technical building in years 5-8.
claims.detail: GNIAL has 1,000 ha allotted, about 100 ha of it earmarked for an Aerocity. The long-term cargo target is 150,000 t/yr. Revenue share to MIL is 14.49% (snippet). MIL is a 51:49 MADC:AAI joint venture formed in 2009. History: GMR received the letter of award in March 2019, the state cancelled the tender in 2020, the Bombay HC quashed the cancellation, and takeover slipped from April 2025 to June 2026. The GMR NSE filing timed out when I tried to open it, so the handover date comes from search snippets of that filing plus PSU Watch and Outlook Business (opened).
claims.design_takeaway: Real-world planning puts Nagpur at 30-50 Mppa within this century. That is a useful 'baseline Nagpur' figure next to ZMI's merger-scale demand. GMR's own reasoning, Nagpur's central location for cargo, supports ZMI's hub logic and suggests a strong cargo/MRO landside zone.

sources.title: GMR charts Rs 300 crore makeover for Nagpur airport (PSU Watch, 8 Jul 2026)
sources.quote: Opened. Capacity from about 3 million to 30 million over the 30-year concession, scalable to 50 million; 1,000 ha allotted, about 100 ha Aerocity; cargo 150,000 t/yr long-term.

sources.title: GMR Airports unveils multi-phase expansion roadmap for Nagpur airport (Outlook Business/PTI, 9 Jul 2026)
sources.quote: Opened. Phase 2 (years 3-4): new integrated terminal, initial 4 million pax; Phase 3 (years 5-8): second runway, new ATC tower, technical building.

sources.title: GMR Airports NSE filing - Commencement of operations, Nagpur (25 Jun 2026)
sources.quote: Search snippet only (fetch timed out): GNIAL took over operations effective 25 June 2026 after handover of airport assets and operations from MIHAN India Limited.

claims.claim: Sources disagree on the planned second runway at NAG. The 2021 MIL pre-feasibility report and a December 2024 Hitavada report describe a new parallel runway of initially 3,200 m (Code 4E), extended to 4,000 m (Code F) in Phase II, plus a 400 m extension of the existing runway at the runway-32 end. MADC's MIHAN SEZ overview describes a 4,000 × 60 m second runway 1,600 m from the existing runway, which is to be lengthened to 3,600 × 45 m.
claims.detail: Hitavada (29 Dec 2024, opened): MADC to hand over 786 ha to MIL. Airport land rises from 520.83 ha existing plus 865.21 ha to 1,386.04 ha (3,425 acres). The MIHAN SEZ overview gives the airport as 1,364 ha. GMR's 2026 announcements (opened) do not state the runway length. The 2021 PFR's Phase-I terminal is 56,250 m² for 3.475 million passengers (design year 2029-30).
claims.design_takeaway: A 1,600 m separation allows independent parallel operations, and 4,000 m with Code F is the right baseline for ZMI too. A combined-traffic hub would need more independent runways (probably 4-6) and needs its own site. This NAG data is a lower bound, not a template.

sources.title: PFR for the Expansion of Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar International Airport (MIL, 2021)
sources.quote: Opened. "the second runway initial length is of 3200 M suitable for Code 4E"; Phase-II "increase in length of the new runway by 800 meters (to make it 4000 m long runway) catering to the 'Code 4 F'"; existing runway extended by 400 m.

sources.title: MIHAN Project - an Overview (MADC / MIHAN SEZ)
sources.quote: Opened. Existing runway to be extended 200 m to 3,600 x 45 m; parallel second runway 4,000 x 60 m; separation 1,600 m.

sources.title: MADC to hand over 786 ha land to MIL (The Hitavada, 29 Dec 2024)
sources.quote: Opened. "Total land under proposed airport is 1,386.04 hectare (3,425 acres)"; "new parallel runway. Its initial length is 3,200 meter."

claims.claim: MIHAN (Multi-modal International Cargo Hub and Airport at Nagpur) is a Maharashtra Airport Development Company (MADC) project around NAG. MADC gives its total area as 4,354 ha: 1,364 ha airport, 1,238 ha SEZ and 614 ha for rail and road terminals, housing and other uses. Land is allotted to CONCOR for a rail terminal, a road terminal is planned for about 900-1,000 trucks, and JNPT's dry port is under 40 km away.
claims.detail: SEZ area figures conflict: 1,238 ha (MADC overview), 1,236 ha (Hitavada 2022), 1,460 ha (MIL website), 1,511.51 ha notified (Lok Sabha answer, snippet), and 'more than 2,000 Hectares' (district site, last updated 2019). Total area: 4,354 ha (MADC) vs 4,025 ha (Wikipedia). Hitavada (2022, snippet) says more than 40% of the land was still unsold. The Orange Line metro already runs through MIHAN to Khapri (see metro-01).
claims.design_takeaway: MIHAN shows Nagpur's existing policy direction: an airport combined with cargo, a SEZ, rail and road terminals. ZMI can present itself as MIHAN scaled up, and its landside plan should keep a rail freight terminal and truck marshalling separate from passenger approaches.

sources.title: MIHAN Project - an Overview
sources.quote: Opened. Total 4,354 ha; SEZ 1,238 ha; airport 1,364 ha; 614 ha for rail terminal, road terminal, residential etc.; CONCOR rail terminal; road terminal for 1,000 multi-axle trucks; JNPT dry port <40 km.

sources.title: MIHAN - Nagpur district website
sources.quote: Opened. "MADC is developing a huge SEZ on an area of more than 2,000 Hectares"; road terminal for "about 900 trucks at a time"; rail terminal "capable of handling 2 trains at a time".

sources.title: MIHAN India Limited
sources.quote: Opened. "About 1460 hectares allocated for IT, Health, Food, and Logistics sectors."

claims.claim: The Hindu Hrudaysamrat Balasaheb Thackeray Maharashtra Samruddhi Mahamarg (Mumbai-Nagpur Expressway) is a 701 km, six-lane, access-controlled greenfield expressway built by MSRDC. Its design speed is 150 km/h and its right of way is 120 m (90 m in forest). Its Nagpur end is at Shivmadka village in Hingna tehsil, about 23 km from Nagpur, and it ends at Amane (Bhiwandi taluka, Thane district).
claims.detail: Posted limits are lower than the design speed: 120 km/h on flat terrain and 100 km/h in ghat sections (The Week/PTI 2025). It crosses 10 districts, 26 talukas and 392 villages, with 25 interchanges (IC/01 Nagpur to IC/25 Bhiwandi) per themetrorailguy; one other source says 24. Cost is about Rs 55,000 crore (55,335 crore per a Free Press Journal snippet). No source I found uses the term 'zero point' for Shivmadka, and none confirms its exact distance from MIHAN or Butibori. My search budget ran out before I could pin this down. Swarajya says the Shivmadka end 'currently serves as the outer bypass to the city'.
claims.design_takeaway: The expressway's Nagpur terminus lies on the south-west of the city, the same side as MIHAN, NH44 and Butibori. A ZMI site in this south-west quadrant could take a direct expressway spur from IC/01, bringing the Mumbai catchment in by road in about 8 hours. The 120 m right of way also reserves space for the planned HSR, which follows the same alignment.

sources.title: Mumbai-Nagpur Expressway - Information & Status (The Metro Rail Guy)
sources.quote: Opened. 701 km, 6 lanes, "designed for a top speed of 150 kmph", from village Shivmadka in Nagpur district to village Amne in Thane district; 120 m broad; 25 interchanges.

sources.title: India's fastest highway... (Swarajya)
sources.quote: Opened. "the new highway begins in a small village, Shivmadka in Hingna tehsil located at a distance of 23 km away from Nagpur"; "designed for a top speed of 150 km per hour".

sources.title: Samruddhi Mahamarg to be a game-changer: CM (The Hitavada, 5 Dec 2022)
sources.quote: Opened. Leaders began the drive from "village Shivmadka in Hingna tehsil of Nagpur district".

claims.claim: Samruddhi opened in four stages: Nagpur-Shirdi (520 km) on 11 December 2022, inaugurated by PM Modi; Shirdi-Bharvir (80 km) on 26 May 2023; Bharvir-Igatpuri (25 km) on 4 March 2024; and Igatpuri-Amane (76 km) on 5 June 2025. The full 701 km has been open since 5 June 2025, cutting Nagpur-Mumbai road time to about 8 hours from about 17-18.
claims.detail: The length of the first stage is given as 520 km (PIB/PMO, The Week, Hitavada) or 502 km (Swarajya, themetrorailguy). 520 km is the official figure. The last stretch was delayed from its expected October/November 2024 opening because the spur road to the Vadodara-Mumbai Expressway was not finished.
claims.design_takeaway: The road link to Mumbai is real and finished, which supports a scenario where BOM traffic shifts to a central hub. In the game, 'Samruddhi corridor' can be the main road feed, at about 8 hours from Mumbai.

sources.title: Final stretch of 701-km-long Mumbai-Nagpur Samruddhi Expressway opened (The Week/PTI, 5 Jun 2025)
sources.quote: Opened. Final 76 km Igatpuri-Amane opened 5 Jun 2025; Phase 1 520 km on 11 Dec 2022; Shirdi-Bharvir 80 km on 26 May 2023; Bharvir-Igatpuri 25 km on 4 Mar 2024; about 8 hours vs about 18 hours.

sources.title: PMO/PIB release, 11 Dec 2022
sources.quote: Search snippet only: PM inaugurated Phase I of the Hindu Hrudaysamrat Balasaheb Thackeray Maharashtra Samruddhi Mahamarg covering 520 km connecting Nagpur and Shirdi; full project 701 km.

claims.claim: Maharashtra plans to extend the Samruddhi network east and south from the Nagpur/Wardha end: Nagpur-Bhandara-Gondia and Nagpur-Gadchiroli spurs (announced in the 2021-22 plans and the 2022 state budget), and the Nagpur-Goa 'Shaktipeeth' expressway starting at Pavnar in Wardha district, linked to Samruddhi near the Digras interchange.
claims.detail: Construction status is not confirmed. A February 2024 report cited about Rs 60,000 crore for the expansions, including a 141 km Nagpur-Gondia expressway (snippet). The Shaktipeeth endpoint is given as either Patradevi or Banda (Sindhudurg). A land-portal source says the alignment was revised from 802.6 km to 856.8 km on 1 April 2026, which I could not verify officially. These are planned projects.
claims.design_takeaway: Nagpur is becoming the junction of a radial expressway network: west to Mumbai, east to Gondia and Gadchiroli, south-west to Goa. A ZMI landside plan can show a multi-spoke 'zero mile' road diagram with the hub at the junction.

sources.title: State Budget: Samruddhi Mahamarg to be extended upto Gadchiroli (The Hitavada, 2022)
sources.quote: Search snippet only: extension of Samruddhi Mahamarg up to Gadchiroli; Nagpur to Bhandara-Gondia and Nagpur to Gadchiroli.

sources.title: Maharashtra government greenlights Rs 84,000 crore Shaktipeeth Expressway (Swarajya)
sources.quote: Search snippet only: Shaktipeeth expressway from Pavnar in Wardha district to Sindhudurg.

claims.claim: The Mumbai-Nagpur high-speed rail corridor is still a proposal, not a sanctioned project. NHSRCL completed surveys and submitted a DPR to the Railway Ministry in about 2022, costed at about Rs 1.7 lakh crore. The line would run parallel to Samruddhi with about 15 stations, including 'Khapri Depot'. As of February 2026 the DPR was reported as 'under examination'.
claims.detail: Length is variously given as 741 km (DPR report, Sept 2023), 753 km or 766 km (Nov 2021). Target journey time is about 3.5-4 hours at over 300 km/h (320 km/h in one snippet). Stations named in reports include Shahapur, Igatpuri, Nashik, Shirdi, Sambhajinagar, Jalna, Mehkar, Malegaon Jahangir, Karanja Lad, Pulgaon, Wardha, Khapri Depot and Nagpur. The Nagpur terminal location (Khapri, Ajni or MIHAN) is not confirmed in any source I found. The Union Budget 2026-27 announced seven new HSR corridors and Mumbai-Nagpur was not among them (Indian Express, 10 Feb 2026, via SuperKalam). Because it would run along the Samruddhi alignment, land need is only about 1,250 ha.
claims.design_takeaway: A 'Khapri Depot' station near MIHAN and NH44 is the most natural place for an HSR station at a south-Nagpur hub. ZMI could include an integrated HSR station under the terminal, as at Frankfurt or Paris-CDG. The roadmap should mark it as speculative, since the line is unsanctioned. A 3.5-hour Mumbai link is what makes closing BOM at all believable.

claims.claim: NH44, India's longest national highway at about 4,112 km from Srinagar to Kanyakumari, runs through Nagpur. South of the city it follows Wardha Road past the airport (0.31 km away) and MIHAN to Butibori. A Rs 619.55 crore six-lane flyover of 2.69 km between Chinchbhuvan and the MIHAN interchange, with service roads, was started in about November 2025 with a 24-month target.
claims.detail: The 4,112 km length comes from Wikipedia and Housing.com (snippets), and older figures give 3,745 km. The flyover facts come from search snippets of Swarajya and Constrofacilitator. The Chinchbhuvan-Jamtha flyover bhoomipujan was in March 2024 (Hitavada, snippet). The NHAI widening is a 3.05 km six-lane stretch near the MIHAN interchange. Butibori flyover was dedicated in June 2021, and a 2021 promise to make Nagpur-Butibori six-lane within 6 months does not appear to have been met. Nagpur also has an Outer Ring Road that connects to the Samruddhi end. I did not open its exact geometry.
claims.design_takeaway: NH44 is the north-south spine (Delhi-Nagpur-Hyderabad-Bengaluru), which suits a hub replacing BLR and HYD feeder demand. Wardha Road is already congested, so ZMI's landside should keep airport traffic on a dedicated grade-separated spur off NH44, Samruddhi and the ORR, not on Wardha Road itself.

Status of the Wardha-Nagpur 3rd and 4th rail lines after their February 2026 target, and whether an airport or MIHAN station on the main line is planned.

I found no Nagpur-specific geotechnical data (swell pressure, depth of the active zone, depth to basalt) for the MIHAN-Butibori belt. Peer-reviewed or VNIT/IGS sources would be needed for a credible foundation strategy.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Nagpur's Zero Mile monument has two sandstone elements. One is a pillar. The other is a small stone marking a Great Trigonometrical Survey (GTS) Standard Bench Mark, inscribed "G.T.S. STANDARD BENCH MARK. 1907". An inscription records the pillar top as 1,020.171 ft (310.948 m) above mean sea level. The site is south-east of the Vidhan Bhavan (state legislature building) in central Nagpur.
verdicts.note: I opened The Better India, Hitavada 2023, Incredible India and Wikipedia. Hitavada 2023 gives 'two sandstone structures, a pillar and a small stone' and says the small stone 'depicts GTS Standard Bench Mark'. Better India gives both inscriptions and the SE-of-Vidhan-Bhavan location, but it takes the inscription wording from a visitor's blog. The conversion checks out: 1,020.171 ft x 0.3048 = 310.948 m. The hexagonal-base distance table (Raipur 174 mi and so on) is only on Wikipedia. Better India and Incredible India say only that distances are engraved, so cite the table as Wikipedia-only. Process caveat: the shared WebSearch budget ran out after my first query. All my checks used direct fetches of the cited pages and of primary documents (IMD, CGWB, MIDC, Central Railway, NSE). I could not run fresh searches for contradicting sources.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Four stucco horses stand beside the stone. Hitavada (2025) says they were 'added quite later' but gives no date or builder. In January 2023 (reported 11 Jan 2023 as approved 'on Tuesday') the Heritage Conservation Committee approved CREDAI Nagpur's plan covering 'the four horses, sand stone, and the Zero Mile pillar'. By then two of the horses had developed cracks. In March 2025 the HCC directed NMC to send a proposal to the Maharashtra government, through the Urban Development Department, to transfer custody of the monument to NMC; at present the District Collectorate oversees it. The PWD had been entrusted with renovation and restoration. CM Devendra Fadnavis had asked Indian Oil to fund it from CSR, and per the article those funds are for beautifying the surrounding area.
verdicts.note: The facts hold, but the mechanism is slightly different. NMC is to propose to the state government that custody be transferred to it. It is not a direct request to the Collectorate. Hitavada 2023 already calls them 'four stucco horses'; only the 2025 piece says they were added later. I could not verify the 2008 Times of India maintenance pledge beyond Wikipedia.

verdicts.corrected_claim: The usual account is that the British erected the monument during the Raj in connection with the Great Trigonometrical Survey, and the benchmark stone is dated 1907. No source I found names a specific agency, officer or date for the pillar itself, as distinct from the benchmark.
verdicts.note: Better India says only 'constructed during the time of the Raj'. Incredible India links it to the GTS but gives no date. Hitavada 2023 ('built during British time to mark the Trigonometric Survey of India in 1907') and Wikipedia ('built by the British during the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India in 1907') do put 1907 on the monument. They appear to take it from the benchmark inscription, and neither names a builder. Hitavada 2025's 'at the time of start of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India in the year 1907' is chronologically wrong. Wikipedia's GTS article (pointer only) says the survey 'started on 10 April 1802' under William Lambton and was completed in 1871 under James Walker.

verdicts.corrected_claim: It is widely said that the Zero Mile stone marks the geographic centre of (colonial) India, but this is contested and not officially verified. The Government of India's tourism site calls the claim 'debatable'. Two Madhya Pradesh villages, Karaundi (described by The Better India as about 40 km from Sihora in Jabalpur district) and Barsali (Betul district), are put forward as the centre of post-1947 India.
verdicts.note: This claim is well supported, and its 'low' confidence label looks too pessimistic; 'medium-high' is closer. Incredible India: 'debatable'. Better India: Karaundi 'about 40 km from Sihora in Jabalpur district'. Wikipedia names Karaundi and Barsali, and its Barsali page puts Barsali in Betul tehsil, Betul district, so the Betul attribution rests on Wikipedia only. Caveat: Katni district was carved out of Jabalpur in 1998, and Karaundi may now be in Katni. I could not check that, so use 'near Sihora, Jabalpur/Katni area'. Hitavada's 'equidistant nine metros' is false. My great-circle distances from the stone's coordinates (21.1499N, 79.0806E) are: Hyderabad about 423 km, Pune about 620 km, Mumbai CSMIA about 688 km, Ahmedabad SVPIA about 698 km, Delhi about 851 km, Bengaluru KIA about 896 km, Chennai about 906 km, Kolkata about 971 km, Kochi about 1,283 km. These are my own haversine calculations, not a published source. MIHAN India's site confirms the 'Connecting miles through zero mile' tagline.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Nagpur's all-time highest temperature is 47.9 °C, recorded in late May 2013. Al Jazeera reported it on 23 May 2013, and the IMD sheet reportedly dates it 23 May; I could not open that sheet, and the afternoon reading may have been on 22 May. The previous record was 47.8 °C on 26 May 1954. IMD's 'Extremes of temperature and rainfall up to 2012' lists that as the highest maximum for Nagpur (Sonegaon). The district website's '48.6 °C on 29 May 2012' is contradicted by IMD's extremes table, which runs to 2012 and has no reading above 47.8 °C.
verdicts.note: I independently confirmed the 1954 previous record from IMD Pune's extremes publication, opened and text-extracted: Nagpur (Sonegaon) (A), May, Tx 47.8, date 26, 1954. Nagpur (Mayo Hospital) shows 47.7 °C on 26 May 1954. IMD's 1981-2010 normals also give 47.8 °C (26 May 1954) as the annual highest, so 47.9 °C in 2013 is the new record. Al Jazeera (23 May 2013) has the 47.9 °C reading. imdnagpur.gov.in refused connections twice, so the exact '23 May' date is still from a snippet. The Wikipedia climate box (extremes 1901-2020) also gives a 47.9 °C record high for May. Its text claim of '47 °C on 30 May 2024' as the record is internally inconsistent; ignore it.

verdicts.corrected_claim: May is Nagpur's hottest month. IMD's 1981-2010 normals for Nagpur (Sonegaon) give a May mean daily maximum of 42.7 °C and mean daily minimum of 27.8 °C. The 1991-2020 normals, as reproduced on Wikipedia citing IMD and the Tokyo Climate Center, give 43.1 °C and 28.1 °C. Record maxima cluster in late May (26 May 1954, May 2013). Per IMD data reported by The Hitavada (11 May 2022), Nagpur has more heat-wave days than any other Maharashtra city: 107 in May and 246 in all over 1969-2019, ahead of Chandrapur (90) and Yavatmal (80).
verdicts.note: The claimed pair '43.1 / 27.8' mixes two normal periods. The 43.1 max matches 1991-2020 and the 27.8 min matches 1981-2010. Unless the IMD May sheet, which I could not open, uses its own period, give the pair from one period. 'Peak usually in last week of May' is not directly verified, but the record dates support it. The heat-wave counts and thresholds are confirmed from Hitavada: plains threshold 40 °C; heat wave at a departure of 4.5-6.4 °C or an absolute ≥45 °C; severe at >6.4 °C departure or ≥47 °C.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Nagpur's normal annual rainfall is about 1,100 mm: 1,100.3 mm over 56.6 rainy days in IMD's 1981-2010 normals for Sonegaon, and about 1,151 mm for 1991-2020 per Wikipedia. Most of it, about 84% (919.7 mm), falls in the south-west monsoon from June to September, with July the wettest month at 313.7 mm. IMD Nagpur says the normal onset date has moved from 10 June to 15 June.
verdicts.note: 'Nearly all' overstates it: June-September is 168.8 + 313.7 + 267.0 + 170.2 = 919.7 mm of 1,100.3 mm, about 84%. Other figures: CGWB gives a district normal of 1,000-1,200 mm, rising from Katol (985.4 mm) in the west to Umrer (1,213.6 mm) in the east. The district website gives 1,064.1 mm, alongside an inconsistent 1,205 mm for June-September. The onset change is confirmed: Hitavada quotes M L Sahu, DDG at IMD's Nagpur regional office. The 'withdrawal around early October' was a 2021 forecast ('after October 7-8'), not a normal date. The IMD Pune Maharashtra 88.4% figure is unverified (snippet only).

verdicts.corrected_claim: Before the monsoon, Vidarbha including Nagpur gets afternoon and evening thunderstorms, sometimes with hail and gusts of 40-50 km/h. IMD issued an orange alert for all of Vidarbha on 9-10 April 2024, and a yellow alert, not orange, for 7-9 May 2024, when hail fell in parts of Nagpur. IMD's 1981-2010 normals for Nagpur (Sonegaon) put these risks in numbers: about 50 thunderstorm days a year (4.0 in April, 6.2 in May, 9.5 in June), 1.9 squall days, 0.3 dust-storm days and only 0.1 hail days a year.
verdicts.note: The May 2024 alert was yellow: the Hitavada article says "issued 'yellow alert' all over Vidarbha". The researcher gave no source for '3-4 April 2025', so it is unverified. The 'no data on dust storms' gap can be closed: IMD's climatological table lists days with hail, thunder, fog, dust storm and squall. Dust storms (0.3 days a year) and hail (0.1 days a year, recorded in March) are statistically rare. Thunderstorms are frequent.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Deccan Trap basalt is Nagpur district's main rock formation, covering about 4,300 km² of the 9,892 km² district. Archaean crystalline rocks (gneiss, schist) occur in the north-east and south-east. Gondwana sediments cover about 470 km² from Kamptee to Saoner, Lameta beds form a small northern patch, and alluvium more than 25 m thick lies in the south from Butibori to Bela. Soils are mixed: medium to deep clayey black cotton soils, medium loamy alluvial soils, and shallow sandy or clayey red soils. The ICAR-CRIDA split of 43% deep, 14% medium-deep and 43% shallow black soil could not be verified.
verdicts.note: The geology list does not come from the CGWB 2022 aquifer PDF the researcher cited. That file is an 84-page annexure, and its text does not mention Lameta or Archaean. The list is in CGWB's 2013 district brochure, which I opened. 'Soils are black soils of varying depth' overstates it, since CGWB lists six soil types, including red and alluvial soils. The ICAR-CRIDA server refused connections and timed out, so the percentages stay unverified. The annexure does record 'Black cotton soil' on Deccan trap at Haladgaon (20.843N, 78.866E), close to the Butibori corridor. I did not verify the swell-shrink behaviour or the IS 2911 practice from any opened source; they are standard engineering knowledge.

research.topic: Airport planning norms and benchmark numbers for Zero Mile International (ZMI): runway spacing, code F geometry, hot-weather runway length, rapid exit taxiways and runway occupancy, runway capacity and wake separation, MARS stands, walking distances, APMs, minimum connecting times, traffic benchmarks, kerb sizing

claims.claim: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I (8th ed., July 2018), Recommendation 3.1.12, recommends these minimum distances between the centre lines of parallel instrument runways used at the same time: 1,035 m for independent parallel approaches, 915 m for dependent parallel approaches, 760 m for independent parallel departures and 760 m for segregated parallel operations.
claims.detail: For segregated operations, the 760 m 'may be decreased by 30 m for each 150 m that the arrival runway is staggered toward the arriving aircraft, to a minimum of 300 m'. It 'should be increased by 30 m for each 150 m' of stagger away from the arriving aircraft. For independent approaches, other combinations of distance and conditions may be applied if a safety assessment supports them. The procedures are in PANS-ATM (Doc 4444) Ch. 6 and PANS-OPS (Doc 8168); guidance is in the SOIR manual (Doc 9643). These are Recommendations, not Standards. I read the Annex 14 PDF directly.
claims.design_takeaway: Use 1,035 / 915 / 760 / 760 m as the hard floor in the ZMI geometry generator. Because 760 m can be reduced or must be increased with stagger, offsetting thresholds is a design lever the game can show.

claims.claim: PANS-ATM 6.7.3 ties independent parallel approaches to surveillance performance that depends on spacing. From 1,035 m to under 1,310 m: SSR azimuth accuracy of 0.06 deg (or 30 m MLAT/ADS-B), an update period of 2.5 s or less, and a high-resolution display with position prediction and deviation alert. From 1,310 m to under 1,525 m: an update period of 5 s or less. At 1,525 m or more: standard SSR (0.3 deg) with an update period of 5 s or less. Below 1,525 m, independent approaches must be suspended in certain weather (wind shear, turbulence, crosswind, thunderstorms).
claims.detail: Other PANS-ATM conditions: a no-transgression zone (NTZ) at least 610 m wide, set equidistant between the extended centre lines; precision approach or qualifying RNP AR / APV procedures; and missed-approach tracks diverging by at least 30 deg. Independent departures (760 m) need departure tracks diverging by 15 deg immediately after take-off, or 10 deg if both are RNAV/RNP with the turn starting within 2 NM, plus surveillance that identifies aircraft within 1 NM of the runway end. Segregated operations need the departure track to diverge by at least 30 deg from the adjacent missed-approach track. Dependent approaches (915 m+) need diagonal separation of 2.0 NM (courses more than 2,529 m apart), 1.5 NM (1,097 to 2,529 m) or 1.0 NM (915 to 1,097 m). Source: a CASA (Australia) table that reproduces the PANS-ATM text, which I opened. On the brief's 'older 1,525 m minimum': 1,525 m is no longer the minimum, but it is still the threshold for standard surveillance and for the weather-suspension rule. I did not verify the history of 1,525 m as the earlier minimum.
claims.design_takeaway: ZMI's 1,550 m outer-middle spacing clears the 1,525 m threshold by only 25 m. That margin is what lets those approaches use ordinary 5 s radar and stay independent in monsoon wind shear and thunderstorms, so treat 1,550 m as a minimum and do not let geometry tweaks shrink it. The 850 m pair can run segregated operations (one runway arriving, one departing) or independent departures. It cannot take simultaneous approaches under ICAO: it is under 915 m, so not even dependent approaches are allowed. The game should block 'both runways landing' on the 850 m pair and require a 30 deg split between departures and missed approaches.

claims.claim: The FAA's 2015 rules (Notice N JO 7110.693, amending JO 7110.65 paras 5-9-6 and 5-9-7) lowered the dual simultaneous independent approach minimum to 3,600 ft (1,097 m). It is 3,000 ft (914 m) with a 2.5 to 3.0 deg offset approach at fields at or below 2,000 ft MSL. Triple approaches need 3,900 ft (1,189 m). A final monitor aid with an update of 4.8 s or better is required for dual runways 3,000 to 4,300 ft apart, and PRM approaches must be assigned below 4,300 ft. Dependent approaches are allowed from 2,500 to 9,000 ft apart.
claims.detail: The brief's '4,300 ft / 3,400 ft with PRM' figures are the older standard. A DTIC report on the earlier 7110.65R gives 4,300 ft for standard dual approaches and 3,400 ft for PRM (3,000 ft with a localizer offset over 2.5 deg); I saw this only in a search snippet. Under the 2015 rules, dependent approaches use diagonal separation of 1 NM at 2,500 to 3,600 ft, 1.5 NM at more than 3,600 to 4,300 ft, and 2 NM at more than 4,300 to 9,000 ft. The notice ran from 17 Aug 2015 and was cancelled 26 May 2016 on incorporation into the order. faa.gov blocked the current 7110.65 HTML page (403), so I have not checked the current paragraph text directly. In FAA terms, 1,550 m = 5,085 ft and 850 m = 2,789 ft.
claims.design_takeaway: Under FAA rules the 1,550 m spacing exceeds even the 5,000 ft triple-approach threshold above which no final monitor aid is needed. The 850 m pair (2,789 ft) could take dependent approaches with 1 NM diagonal stagger, which ICAO (915 m) does not allow. An Indian site would follow DGCA/ICAO, so design to ICAO and mention the FAA difference only as a footnote.

claims.claim: Annex 14 Table 3-1 (8th ed., 2018) gives these taxiway minimum separation distances. Code F: taxiway centre line to instrument runway centre line (code 3 or 4) 180 m; taxiway to taxiway 91 m; taxiway (other than stand taxilane) to object 51 m; stand taxilane to stand taxilane 87.5 m; stand taxilane to object 47.5 m. Code E: 172.5 / 76 / 43.5 / 72.5 / 40 m. Code C: 158 / 44 / 26 / 40.5 / 22.5 m.
claims.detail: These are the post-2018 values (Amendment 14, applicable 8 Nov 2018). Older documents give larger code F figures: a 2005 ICAO working paper lists 190 m runway-to-taxiway and 97.5 m taxiway-to-taxiway, and 50.5 m was the old stand-taxilane-to-object total. The brief's '50.5 m' is therefore the superseded value; 51 m is the current taxiway-to-object figure. Notes to Table 3-1: the taxiway-to-taxiway distance 'does not necessarily provide the capability of making a normal turn' onto a parallel taxiway, and the runway-taxiway distances do not guarantee room behind a holding aircraft for another to pass on a parallel taxiway. I read the table directly from the Annex PDF.
claims.design_takeaway: Use 180 m runway-to-taxiway and 91 m taxiway-to-taxiway for code F everywhere in the ZMI apron and taxiway generator. The 850 m runway pair can hold a dual parallel code F taxiway system: 180 + 91 + 180 = 451 m, leaving about 400 m for holding bays, de-icing or end-around taxiways. Check the generator's current numbers against the 2018 values, not the pre-2018 ones.

claims.claim: Annex 14 code letters by wingspan: C = 24 m to under 36 m; D = 36 to under 52 m; E = 52 to under 65 m; F = 65 to under 80 m. Example aircraft: A320neo 35.80 m and 737-8 35.90 m (code C); 787-9 60.1 m, 777-300ER 64.8 m and A350-900 64.75 m (code E); A380 79.75 m (code F). The 777-9 spans 71.8 m with wingtips extended (code F runway) and 64.85 m folded, so it taxis and parks as code E.
claims.detail: Table 1-1 and the A380 span (79.75 m, from Airbus's Aircraft Characteristics document, Rev. Dec 2023) were read directly. The A320neo, 737-8, 787-9, 777-300ER, A350 and 777-9 spans come from search snippets (SKYbrary, Boeing airport brochures, Lufthansa fleet page, The Air Current, Aeroxplorer), not from opened manufacturer pages. Boeing's own site blocked direct download. I did not verify an A330 span in this pass; the A330 is code E in common references. The 2018 Annex 14 also changed runway width to depend on code number plus outer main gear wheel span: 45 m for code 4 with OMGWS 9 to 15 m. Total runway-plus-shoulder width must be 75 m for code F four-engine aircraft and 60 m for code F twins. The precision runway strip extends 140 m each side of the centre line (code 3/4).
claims.design_takeaway: The design fleet's limit is the A380 at 79.75 m, just under the 80 m code F ceiling. Most widebodies (787, A350, 777-300ER and the folded 777-9) are code E, so mark only a minority of stands, and only the runways and taxiways they need, as code F. Use 45 m runways with 75 m total width including shoulders, not the pre-2018 60 m runway width.

claims.claim: ICAO's Aerodrome Design Manual Part 1 (Doc 9157, 4th ed. 2020, para 3.5) says that, when flight-manual data are not available, the basic runway length should be increased by 7% per 300 m of elevation. It should then be increased by a further 1% for every 1 deg C by which the aerodrome reference temperature exceeds the standard-atmosphere temperature at that elevation. If the combined correction exceeds 35%, a specific study is required.
claims.detail: Aerodrome reference temperature = T1 + (T2 - T1)/3. T1 is the monthly mean of the average daily temperature for the hottest month; T2 is the monthly mean of the daily maximum for that month. Standard atmosphere is 15.0 deg C at 0 m and 11.75 deg C at 500 m. Read directly from Doc 9157 Part 1 (Swiss FOCA-hosted copy).
claims.design_takeaway: For a Nagpur-area site at about 315 m: the elevation correction is about 7.35%. With a hottest-month mean maximum of about 43 deg C and an assumed mean daily temperature of about 35 deg C, the reference temperature is about 37.7 deg C. That is about 25 deg C above the standard atmosphere at 315 m (about 13 deg C), so the temperature correction is about 25%. The total is about 32 to 33%, close to the 35% 'specific study' trigger. This is my estimate, and T1 was assumed, not sourced. A 3,100 m sea-level/ISA basic length grows to roughly 4,100 m, which supports 4,000 m-plus long-haul runways at ZMI.

claims.claim: A 2010 LAX take-off length analysis (Ricondo & Associates for Los Angeles World Airports), using manufacturer manuals, gives take-off distances at MTOW at LAX (near sea level). A380-800 at 1,234,588 lb (about 560 t), GP7270 engines: 9,300 ft (2,835 m) at ISA and 9,600 ft (2,926 m) at ISA+15 deg C. 777-300 at 775,000 lb with GE90-115B: 10,200 ft (3,109 m) at ISA and 10,700 ft (3,261 m) at ISA+15. A340-300: 11,500 / 12,100 ft.
claims.detail: The '777-300' row's MTOW (775,000 lb) and engine (GE90-115B) match the 777-300ER. ISA+15 at sea level is 30 deg C, well below Nagpur's summer peaks. Nagpur facts: the IMD May mean maximum is 43.1 deg C, and the record is 47.9 deg C on 23 May 2013 (search snippets of the IMD Nagpur climate sheet and Hindustan Times; the IMD server refused a direct connection). Nagpur airport is about 315 m (1,033 ft) AMSL with a 3,200 m x 45 m runway (MIHAN operator page, snippet). A SKYbrary snippet gives a rule of thumb of about 120 ft of density altitude per deg C above ISA. On that basis, 45 deg C at Nagpur (about ISA+32) means a density altitude of roughly 1,000 + 3,800 = about 4,800 ft (my calculation). I found no published 777-300ER or A380 figures at 45 deg C. Hamad (Doha) has a 4,850 m runway (airport-technology snippet), but I found no source tying that length to heat.
claims.design_takeaway: Even at ISA+15 a full 777-300ER needs about 3.3 km at sea level, and Nagpur's 43 to 47 deg C summers add a further large penalty. A 4,000 to 4,500 m length for the long-haul runways is defensible. The game can model summer-afternoon payload limits, or push heavy long-haul departures to night slots, as the Gulf hubs do.

claims.claim: Annex 14 (3.9.15 to 3.9.18) recommends that a rapid exit taxiway for code number 3 or 4 have a turn-off curve radius of at least 550 m, to allow exit speeds of 93 km/h in wet conditions. Its intersection angle with the runway should be between 25 and 45 deg, preferably 30 deg. It should include a straight section after the turn-off curve long enough for the aircraft to stop clear of any crossing taxiway.
claims.detail: For code 1 and 2 the figures are 275 m radius and 65 km/h. Guidance on where to place rapid exits is in Doc 9157 Part 2. Read directly from the Annex.
claims.design_takeaway: Draw ZMI's rapid exits at 30 deg with a 550 m radius. The straight section after the curve has to fit inside the 180 m runway-to-taxiway offset (code F), which limits how far down the runway exits can sit and still let aircraft stop clear of the parallel taxiway.

claims.claim: An average arrival runway occupancy time (ROT) of 50 s is the regulatory threshold for reducing in-trail spacing on final from 3 NM to 2.5 NM. FAA JO 7210.3 para 10-4-9 allows 2.5 NM within 10 NM of the runway if average ROT is 50 s or less, measured over at least 250 arrivals representative of the fleet mix and re-validated within 30 days of significant changes. PANS-ATM 8.7.3 has an equivalent ICAO provision, which also requires surveillance with an update of 5 s or less and good braking action.
claims.detail: I read the FAA notice N JO 7210.765 (eff. 14 Mar 2011) directly. I saw the PANS-ATM wording only in search snippets (an ICAO APAC/EUROCONTROL 2025 workshop deck and EUROCONTROL's ROT page); icao.int blocked direct fetch. EUROCONTROL notes the 50 s condition is commonly read as applying to all arriving traffic. A snippet of a 1979 MITRE/FAA study gave 50 s for 2.5 NM and 37 s for 2.0 NM. SESAR has since validated 2 NM minimum radar separation.
claims.design_takeaway: Use about 50 s as the target arrival ROT in the ZMI engine, achieved with well-placed 30 deg rapid exits. If a runway's simulated ROT goes above 50 s, the engine should drop to 3 NM spacing, which gives the player a concrete reason to build rapid exits.

claims.claim: ICAO wake turbulence minima. Arrivals, distance-based: Heavy behind Heavy 4 NM, Medium behind Heavy 5 NM, Light behind Heavy 6 NM, Light behind Medium 5 NM. Behind an A380 (Super), per the 2008 ICAO state guidance: Heavy 6 NM, Medium 7 NM, Light 8 NM. Departures, time-based (PANS-ATM Doc 4444): behind a Super, 120 s for a Heavy and 180 s for a Medium or Light; behind a Heavy, 120 s for a Medium or Light; behind a Medium, 120 s for a Light. Add 60 s if the follower departs from an intermediate point on the runway.
claims.detail: The arrival table is from EUROCONTROL's RECAT-EU document, Table 1; the departure matrix is from a SESAR Innovation Days 2025 deck that reproduces PANS-ATM. Disagreement: a SKYbrary snippet says current PANS-ATM gives 5 NM for Heavy behind Super, while the EU (AMC7 to Reg. 2020/469) and the FAA (JO 7110.65) use 6 NM. So the brief's '2 min behind heavy, 3 min behind A380' holds for Medium and Light followers, but a Heavy behind an A380 needs only 2 min. The brief's '3 min behind A380' does not apply to Heavy followers. The EUROCONTROL LORD paper gives Medium (A320) behind Heavy as 5 NM, about 124 s, under ICAO.
claims.design_takeaway: Departures stacked behind a Super lose about 60 s compared with a Heavy leader. ZMI's scheduler should cluster A380 departures, or put them at the end of a bank, rather than mix them through medium jet waves. Same-runway intersection departures carry a 60 s penalty.

claims.claim: RECAT-EU (EUROCONTROL, Ed. 1.1, July 2015) replaces ICAO's 3 categories with 6: A Super Heavy, B Upper Heavy, C Lower Heavy, D Upper Medium, E Lower Medium, F Light. Distance minima on approach and departure range from 3 to 8 NM; for example, A to B 4 NM, B to D 4 NM, C to D 3 NM, A to F 8 NM. Time-based departure minima range from 80 to 180 s; for example, A to B 100 s, B to D 100 s, C to D 80 s. EUROCONTROL cites a peak throughput gain of 5% or more, up to 8% at the most constrained airports.
claims.detail: Pairs marked (*) fall back to 2.5 NM minimum radar separation. Paris-CDG reported a gain of 2 to 4 movements per hour at peak after introducing RECAT-EU (search snippet). Read directly from the RECAT-EU PDF; that copy is hosted on code7700.com but is the EUROCONTROL document.
claims.design_takeaway: ZMI is a 2040s-era design, so it should assume RECAT-EU or pairwise separation in its capacity model. A switch between ICAO and RECAT-EU modes is a neat upgrade mechanic.

claims.claim: The FAA's 2018 capacity profile for Atlanta (five parallel runways: three arrival, two departure in East flow) gives a sustainable hourly capacity of 250 to 252 operations in visual conditions, 242 to 248 in marginal, 200 to 204 in instrument and about 177 to 184 in low-instrument conditions. That is roughly 50 operations per runway-hour in VMC and 40 in IMC.
claims.detail: West flow, visual: 231 to 240 operations per hour. Atlanta uses 2.5 NM reduced arrival separation and same-runway departure fanning. The figure is a range between the ATC-reported rate and the model estimate, and reflects ASPM data from Oct 2014 to Sep 2017. The FAA projects 260 operations per hour with improved runway delivery accuracy and Wake RECAT Phase 2. For a single mixed-mode runway: Gatwick declares 55 movements per hour and has delivered 58 in an hour (International Airport Review snippet); a CAPA analyst calls it the only single-runway airport that routinely exceeds 50 per hour (snippet). I did not verify per-runway arrival-only rates (for example Heathrow in segregated mode) because the search budget ran out.
claims.design_takeaway: Calibrate the ZMI engine to about 50 movements per runway-hour in good weather and about 40 in IMC. A 3-arrival / 2-departure layout like Atlanta's tops out around 250 per hour. If ZMI must carry Delhi + Mumbai + Bengaluru + Hyderabad peaks, the runway count follows directly from these rates.

claims.claim: A MARS stand is one stand position that can take either one widebody aircraft or two narrowbody aircraft side by side, using left and right centre lines (L/R) as well as a central one. Example: Dubai International's AIP stand chart (Aug 2026 AIRAC) designates C51L/C51/C51R, C53L/C53/C53R, C54L/C54/C54R and C55L/C55/C55R as 'Multi Aircraft Ramp System (MARS)'. C51, C53, C54 and C55 are for code F aircraft and 'can be used also for Code D and E only'.
claims.detail: The expansion of the acronym varies: Dubai uses 'Multi Aircraft Ramp System'; the Transoft blog uses 'Multiple Apron Ramp System'; Singapore's AIP supplement calls its F35L/F35R pair 'Multiple Aircraft Receiving Stands' (search snippets). Transoft defines it as serving 'either two smaller aircraft (Code C or smaller) or one larger aircraft (Code D, E, or F)' (snippet). ICAO gives no single formal definition. I read the Dubai chart directly.
claims.design_takeaway: Make most ZMI contact stands MARS: two code C or one code E/F. The 95 m code F module (plan-06) holds two A320neo-size aircraft (2 x 35.8 m + clearances = about 87 m), so the game can flex stand use between narrowbody domestic banks and widebody international banks.

claims.claim: A 2025 National Academies (TRB) report, citing IATA's Airport Development Reference Manual (ADRM, 12th ed., 2022), gives these limits. The maximum acceptable unaided walk between gates is 985 ft (about 300 m, about 5 minutes at 200 ft/min, i.e. 1.0 m/s). With moving walkways it rises to 2,133 ft (about 650 m, about 7 minutes at a 320 ft/min combined speed, about 1.6 m/s). APMs should be used beyond 2,460 ft (about 750 m) when peak demand exceeds 3,000 passengers per direction per hour.
claims.detail: The brief's '600 to 800 m without assistance' is too generous: per this source, about 300 m is the unaided limit and about 650 m applies only with moving walkways. I did not open the ADRM itself (paywalled). Moving walkway belt speeds: EN 115 standard speeds are 0.50 / 0.60 / 0.75 m/s (snippet of a Polish engineering paper), and Stannah lists 0.5 to 0.75 m/s to BS EN 115-1 (snippet).
claims.design_takeaway: Score each ZMI gate's walking distance against three bands: 300 m (green, unaided), 650 m (amber, walkways required) and 750 m (APM required). Belt speed of about 0.65 m/s plus walking gives about 1.6 m/s, which is the speed to use in the pedestrian model.

claims.claim: Beijing Daxing (Zaha Hadid Architects with ADP Ingenierie, opened Sept 2019) has a radial 'starfish' plan: five piers from a central court, 79 gates with airbridges and a 700,000 m^2 terminal. The farthest gate is about 600 m from the terminal centre, under an 8-minute walk.
claims.detail: The 600 m figure is from chief engineer Guo Yanchi, quoted by China Daily, and is measured 'from the center of the terminal'. Some press (Asia Tatler, Vietnam Airlines' magazine) instead say it is measured from security, which conflicts. ZHA's own page gives only 'less than 8 minutes'. Capacity: 45 million passengers a year initially, 72 million by 2025 and up to 100 million planned (ZHA). 600 m in 8 minutes implies about 1.25 m/s.
claims.design_takeaway: Daxing's 600 m centre-to-farthest-gate is a strong benchmark for ZMI's hub-and-pier geometry. It sits between the 300 m unaided and 650 m walkway limits (plan-19), so a radial plan that keeps every gate within about 600 m of the core can avoid an APM for that terminal. Inter-terminal links at ZMI's scale will still need one.

Airport Improvement gives 59 cars rising to 73 and capacity of 10,000 to 12,000 pphpd. LAX's planned APM is about 2-minute headway and 6,000 pphpd peak with four-car, 200-passenger trains (Wikipedia snippet, low confidence). I found no Denver or Dubai headway figures.

claims.claim: Official minimum connecting times (MCTs) for Mumbai are not public. A May 2025 Network Thoughts analysis used Air India's published Mumbai MCTs as a proxy: domestic to international 90 min, international to domestic 120 min and international to international 75 min, all within T2. CSMIA opened India's first domestic-to-domestic airside transfer facility at T2 in 2022, with CISF security in the transfer area, to cut domestic MCT; no figure in minutes was given.
claims.detail: For Delhi T3 I found no official MCT. Blog figures (low confidence) put same-terminal domestic connections at 60 min (IndiGo) and 90 min (Air India), and cross-terminal at 120 min. International comparisons: a Lufthansa executive quoted by Executive Traveller (2011) said Munich T2's MCT is 30 minutes (snippet only; the site returned 403). Other sources give 40 to 45 min, and Travel Extra gives 30 min domestic / 45 min international. For Dubai, flydubai lists T3-to-T3 at 90 min and 120 min where T2 is involved; third-party guides give 60 to 75 min for Emirates connections within the same concourse (snippets; the flydubai page timed out).
claims.design_takeaway: Use Air India's Mumbai figures (75 / 90 / 120 min) as the baseline that ZMI must beat. A single integrated airside with a domestic-international swing zone, like Munich T2, is the design move that gets toward 30 to 45 min, and the game can score the player on achieved MCT.

claims.claim: ACRP Report 40, 2nd ed. (2024), sizes kerbs by vehicle type, not per passenger. Required length = V x D / 60 x L, where V is hourly vehicles stopping, D is dwell time in minutes and L is stall length. A Poisson design factor of 3.0 (fewer than 5 stalls) down to 1.2 (100 stalls or more) is then applied. Sample stall lengths: 25 ft for private cars and taxis, 30 ft for vans and limos, 50 ft for scheduled buses. Sample dwells: private cars 3.0 min at departures and 5.2 min at arrivals, taxis 2 min, buses 5 min. The target for new kerbs is a utilisation ratio of 1.30 or less (65% of inner plus second lane capacity); 1.70 is acceptable for existing facilities.
claims.detail: Chapter 6 calls kerb capacity insufficient when 'curbside requirements (lengths) are greater than 1.3 times the usable curbside length'. Observed dwell times: private cars 86 to 105 s at departures and 74 to 118 s at arrivals; ride-hailing (TNC) cars 51 to 55 s. I found no authoritative 'metres of kerb per peak-hour passenger' rule. The only ratio found is a small-airport master plan (Eugene, OR) citing 'approximately 1,000 annual enplanements per linear foot of curb frontage' (snippet, low confidence). The old FAA AC 150/5360-13 (1988) recommends at least four lanes beside the terminal kerb to absorb double parking (snippet); it was superseded by AC 150/5360-13A (2018).
claims.design_takeaway: At ZMI's scale the Eugene ratio is absurd: about 100 million annual enplanements gives about 100,000 ft, or about 30 km, of kerb. That is a strong quantitative argument for rail-first access (metro and high-speed rail under the forecourt) and multi-level or island forecourts. Size the remaining road kerb with the ACRP formula from a mode-share split.

777-300ER and A380 take-off field length at 43–47 °C and about 315 m elevation (Nagpur conditions) is not published in anything I could open. It needs the Boeing ACAPS and Airbus AC charts; boeing.com blocked downloads and the Airbus figures are graphs.

Nagpur's hottest-month mean daily temperature (T1), needed for an exact aerodrome reference temperature: the IMD Nagpur server refused connections. The ~37.7 °C reference temperature in plan-07 rests on an assumed T1 of ~35 °C.

Official minimum connecting times for Delhi T3, Mumbai T2, Bengaluru and Hyderabad are not public. The figures found are airline proxies (Air India) or blog numbers. The OAG/IATA MCT database or the airlines' own tables would settle them.
Delhi's busiest-day movements since the 4th runway opened (July 2023): no DIAL or AAI record release found. Figures cited range from 1,400 to 1,500 a day now to 'almost 2,000' planned.
I did not consult the IATA ADRM (12th ed.) directly; its walking-distance and APM thresholds come second-hand via the 2025 National Academies report.

Kerb sizing: I found no authoritative 'metres of kerb per peak-hour passenger' rule. ACRP uses a vehicle-based method, so ZMI needs a mode-share assumption (rail / car / taxi / bus) to size its kerbs.

Whether 1,525 m was historically the ICAO minimum for independent approaches, before 1,035 m, is not verified. 1,525 m survives today as the threshold for standard surveillance and for the weather-suspension rule.

verdicts.corrected_claim: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I (8th ed., July 2018), Recommendation 3.1.12, recommends these minimum distances between the centre lines of parallel instrument runways used at the same time: 1,035 m for independent parallel approaches, 915 m for dependent parallel approaches, 760 m for independent parallel departures and 760 m for segregated parallel operations.
verdicts.note: I downloaded the Annex 14 PDF and extracted its text with pdftotext. 3.1.12 is a Recommendation and gives exactly these four values. The stagger rule matches the claim: the distance may be decreased by 30 m per 150 m of stagger toward the arriving aircraft, to a minimum of 300 m, and should be increased by 30 m per 150 m of stagger away. Clause b) does allow other combinations for independent approaches 'when it is determined that such combinations would not adversely affect the safety'. The Note cites PANS-ATM Ch. 6, PANS-OPS and Doc 9643 (SOIR). The cover confirms 'Eighth Edition, July 2018 ... supersedes, on 8 November 2018'.

verdicts.corrected_claim: PANS-ATM 6.7.3 ties independent parallel approaches to surveillance performance that depends on spacing. From 1,035 m to under 1,310 m: SSR azimuth accuracy of 0.06 deg (or 30 m MLAT/ADS-B), an update period of 2.5 s or less, and a high-resolution display with position prediction and deviation alert. From 1,310 m to under 1,525 m: SSR accuracy of 0.3 deg (or equivalent), an update period of 5 s or less, and a determination that safety is not adversely affected. At 1,525 m or more: 0.3 deg SSR with an update period of 5 s or less. Below 1,525 m, independent approaches shall be suspended in certain weather (wind shear, turbulence, downdrafts, crosswind, thunderstorms).
verdicts.note: I downloaded the CASA Annex B PDF and extracted its text; it reproduces PANS-ATM Table 6-1 and paras 6.7.3.x. Every number checks out: 0.06 deg / 30 m / 2.5 s below 1,310 m; 0.3 deg / 5 s at 1,310 to 1,525 m (with the added 'safety ... not adversely affected' condition); 0.3 deg / 5 s at 1,525 m or more. Also confirmed: NTZ at least 610 m; missed-approach tracks diverging by at least 30 deg (6.7.3.2.1 c); dependent diagonal separation of 2.0 / 1.5 / 1.0 NM with 2,529 m and 1,097 m breakpoints; departures diverging 15 deg, or 10 deg if both are RNAV/RNP with the turn within 2.0 NM; segregated operations with a 30 deg split. The 1,525 m suspension rule (6.7.3.3) is quoted. I could not check the history of 1,525 m as the earlier minimum, because my search budget was exhausted.

verdicts.corrected_claim: FAA Notice N JO 7110.693 (effective 17 Aug 2015, cancelled 26 May 2016 on incorporation into JO 7110.65) sets these rules. Dual simultaneous independent approaches need runway centre lines at least 3,600 ft (1,097 m) apart, or at least 3,000 ft (914 m) apart with a 2.5 to 3.0 deg offset approach at fields at or below 2,000 ft MSL. Triple approaches need 3,900 ft (1,189 m) at fields at or below 2,000 ft MSL, or 3,000 ft with offset approaches. A final monitor aid with a surveillance update rate of at least 4.8 s is required for duals 3,000 to 4,300 ft apart and triples 3,000 to under 5,000 ft apart. PRM approaches must be assigned below 4,300 ft. Dependent approaches use 1 NM diagonal separation at 2,500 to 3,600 ft, 1.5 NM above 3,600 up to 4,300 ft, and 2 NM above 4,300 up to 9,000 ft. The notice's stated change was to remove the high-update-radar requirement for close parallels and add offset approaches. It lowered the threshold for standard-radar operations from 4,300 ft, but it did not lower the absolute minimum: the older PRM standard is reported at 3,400 ft, which I did not verify.
verdicts.note: faa.gov returned 403 to WebFetch, so I downloaded the notice PDF directly and read it. Every number in the claim is in the text: dates, 3,600 / 3,000 ft with offset and the 2,000 ft MSL condition, triple 3,900 ft, FMA at 4.8 s, the note that no FMA is needed above 4,300 ft (dual) or at 5,000 ft or more (triple), PRM below 4,300 ft, and dependent 2,500 to 9,000 ft with 1 / 1.5 / 2 NM. One problem: 'lowered the ... minimum to 3,600 ft' overstates the change. The notice describes it as 'the elimination of high update radar requirements previously articulated as a condition for conducting [PRM]'. 3,600 ft is lower than the old 4,300 ft standard-radar threshold, but higher than the old high-update PRM figure (3,400 ft, which I saw only in the researcher's DTIC snippet). I also did not check the current JO 7110.65 text for changes after 2016.

verdicts.corrected_claim: ICAO's Aerodrome Design Manual Part 1 (Doc 9157, 4th ed. 2020, paras 3.5.1 to 3.5.4) says that, when the flight manual is not available, the basic runway length should be increased by 7% per 300 m of elevation. The resulting length should then be increased by 1% for every 1 deg C by which the aerodrome reference temperature exceeds the standard-atmosphere temperature at that elevation. If the combined correction exceeds 35%, a specific study is required.
verdicts.note: I downloaded the BAZL-hosted Doc 9157 Part 1 (4th ed. 2020) and read 3.5.1 to 3.5.4 and Table 3-1 (15.00 deg C at 0 m, 11.75 deg C at 500 m). The reference temperature is T1 + (T2 - T1)/3, as stated. On the design takeaway: Doc 9157 applies the temperature correction to the elevation-corrected length. Compounded, that is about 1.0735 x 1.247 = about 34%, not 32 to 33%, which is even closer to the 35% trigger. T1 remains an assumption.

verdicts.corrected_claim: An average arrival runway occupancy time (ROT) of 50 s is the regulatory threshold for reducing in-trail spacing on final from 3 NM to 2.5 NM. FAA JO 7210.3 para 10-4-9 allows 2.5 NM within 10 NM of the runway if average ROT is 50 s or less, measured over at least 250 arrivals representative of the fleet mix and re-validated within 30 days of significant changes. PANS-ATM 8.7.3 has an equivalent ICAO provision (average ROT not to exceed 50 s, plus other conditions).
verdicts.note: I downloaded the FAA notice and read it; the text matches exactly. The notice ran from 14 Mar 2011 to its cancellation on 25 Aug 2011, once incorporated into JO 7210.3. The EUROCONTROL page (opened) confirms the ICAO 8.7.3 condition of 'not to exceed 50 seconds', notes that it is commonly read as applying to all arriving traffic, and refers to 'all the other criteria from 8.7.3' such as surveillance. I could NOT open PANS-ATM itself, so the specific additional conditions (surveillance update of 5 s or less, good braking action) are unverified here, though consistent with the EUROCONTROL reference.

verdicts.corrected_claim: The FAA's 2018 capacity profile for Atlanta (five parallel runways; East flow uses three for arrivals and two for departures) gives these sustainable hourly capacity ranges in East flow: 250 to 252 operations in visual conditions, 242 to 248 in marginal, 200 to 204 in instrument and 182 to 186 in low instrument. West flow: 231 to 240 visual, 228 to 232 marginal, 197 to 204 instrument and 177 to 178 low instrument. That is roughly 50 operations per runway-hour in VMC and 40 in IMC.
verdicts.note: I downloaded the FAA ATL profile. The visual, marginal and instrument East-flow figures match. The low-instrument figure '177 to 184' is wrong: East flow is 182 to 186 and West flow 177 to 178. Also confirmed: ASPM data from 1 Oct 2014 to 30 Sep 2017 (7am to 11pm); a future of 260 operations per hour in visual East flow with Improved Runway Delivery Accuracy and Wake RECAT Phase 2; and same-runway departure fanning. Reduced 2.5 NM arrival separation is authorized in VMC, marginal and IMC, but 'not available during Low Instrument conditions'. The Gatwick 55 / 58 figures could not be verified: the IAR page I fetched did not mention Gatwick.

verdicts.corrected_claim: ACRP Research Report 266 (2024), 'Airport Curbside and Terminal Area Roadway Operations: New Analysis and Strategies, Second Edition' (the successor to ACRP Report 40), sizes kerbs by vehicle type. Required length = V x D / 60 x L, then a Poisson design factor from 3.0 (fewer than 5 stalls) down to 1.2 (100 stalls or more). Sample stall lengths: 25 ft for private cars and taxis, 30 ft for limousines and vans, 50 ft for scheduled buses. Planning dwells: private cars 3 min at departures and 5.2 min at arrivals, taxis 2 min, buses 5 min. The target for new kerbs is a utilisation ratio of 1.30 or less (65% of inner plus second lane capacity); 1.70 (85%) is acceptable for existing facilities.
verdicts.note: I opened NAP chapters 5 and 6 and the front matter. The publication is ACRP Research Report 266 (2024), second edition, not 'ACRP Report 40, 2nd ed.'. All formula, factor, stall, dwell and ratio values are confirmed, as is the '1.3 times the usable curbside length' trigger in Ch. 6. Observed private-car dwells of 86 to 105 s (departures) and 74 to 118 s (arrivals) are confirmed from Table 5-3. The TNC dwell of 51 to 55 s was not found in the text I could read. The Eugene '1,000 enplanements per linear foot' ratio and the FAA AC 150/5360-13 four-lane note remain snippet-only.
